Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Rahman [Azza wa Jall] is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: except for one verse in it, which is His saying, "Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him" (55:29). It has seventy-six verses. Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said: it is entirely Medinan. The first opinion is more sound, because of what 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr narrated, who said: The first person to recite the Qur'an aloud in Mecca after the Prophet (ﷺ) was Ibn Mas'ud. That was because the Companions said: "Quraysh has never heard this Qur'an recited aloud. Who will make them hear it?" Ibn Mas'ud said: "I will." They said: "We fear for you; we want a man who has a clan to protect him." He refused, then stood at the Station (al-Maqam) and said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an" (55:1–2), and he continued, raising his voice with it, while Quraysh was in its assemblies. They paid attention and said: "What is the son of Umm 'Abd saying?" They said: "He is saying what Muhammad claims was revealed to him." Then they beat him until they left marks on his face.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray the dawn prayer at Nakhla, and recited Surat al-Rahman, and a group of jinn passed by and believed in him. In al-Tirmidhi, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from beginning to end, and they were silent. He said: "I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they were better in response than you. Every time I came to His saying, 'So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?' (55:13), they said: 'No, by nothing of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny; to You is the praise.'" He said: this is a strange (gharib) hadith. In this is evidence that it is Meccan, and Allah knows best. It was also narrated that Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Recite to me of what has been revealed to you." He recited to him Surat al-Rahman. He said: "Repeat it." He repeated it three times. He said: "By Allah, indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a sweetness, its lower part is abundant, its upper part is fruitful, and this is not the speech of a human being. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah."

It was also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For everything there is a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is Surat al-Rahman."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The Most Merciful (1), taught the Qur'an (2), created man (3), taught him eloquence (4).
The sun and the moon run by a reckoning (5), and the star and the tree prostrate (6), and the heaven—He raised it and set up the balance (7), that you not transgress in the balance (8), and establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient (9).
And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures (10), in it is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths (11), and grain with its husk and fragrant plants (12). So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? (13)

His saying, Exalted is He: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Amir al-Sha'bi said: "al-Rahman" is the opening of three surahs which, when combined, form a name of Allah, the Exalted: (Alif-Lam-Ra) and (Ha-Mim) and (Nun), so the combined letters are "al-Rahman."

"Taught the Qur'an": that is, He taught it to His Prophet (ﷺ) until he conveyed it to all people. It was revealed when they said: "And what is the Rahman?" It was also said: it was revealed as a reply to the people of Mecca when they said: "He is only taught by a human being," and "the Rahman of Yamama," meaning Musaylima the Liar. So Allah revealed: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "taught the Qur'an" is that He made it easy to be remembered and recited, as He said: "And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance" (54:17). It was also said: He made it a sign of what people are to worship by.

"Created man": Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan said: it means Adam, peace be upon him.

"Taught him eloquence": the names of everything. It was also said: He taught him all languages. Also from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kaysan: "man" here is intended to mean Muhammad (ﷺ), and "eloquence" is the clarification of the lawful from the unlawful, and of guidance from error. It was also said: what has been and what will be, because he explained about the former and the latter and the Day of Judgment. Al-Dahhak said: "al-Bayan" is good and evil. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is what benefits him and what harms him, and Qatada said the same. It was also said: "man" is intended to mean all people, so it is a generic noun, and "eloquence" on this view is speech and understanding, which is among what man is distinguished by over the rest of the animals. al-Suddi said: He taught every people their tongue with which they speak. Yaman said: writing and inscription with the pen, like His saying: "He who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know" (96:4–5).

"The sun and the moon run by a reckoning": that is, they run according to a known computation, so the predicate is omitted. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu Malik said: that is, they run by a reckoning, in mansions which they do not exceed and from which they do not deviate. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kaysan said: it means that by them time and the terms of lives are reckoned, and were it not for the night, the day, the sun and the moon, no one would know how to count anything, even if the whole age were day. al-Suddi said: "bi-husban" is the determination of their terms, meaning they run for terms like the terms of people, so when their term comes they perish. A similar expression is: "Each runs to a specified term" (13:2 / 31:29 / 39:5). al-Dahhak said: "by a measure." Mujahid said: "bi-husban" is like the husban of a millstone, meaning its pivot, they revolve around it like a pivot. Al-husban may be a verbal noun of "hasabtuhu uhsibuhu" (with damma), husban and husbanan, like al-ghufran, al-kufran and al-rujhan, and also "hisaba," meaning I counted it. al-Akhfash said: it may also be the plural of hisab, like shihab and shuhban. Al-husban also means punishment and short arrows, and it has passed in (al-Kahf) (18:40); its singular is husbana. Al-husbana also means a small cushion. From it one says: "hasabtuhu" when I placed a cushion for him, and a poet said:

"...you would have reclined, not cushioned"

meaning not placed on a cushion, meaning not honoured nor shrouded.

"And the star and the tree prostrate": Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the star is that which has no stalk, and the tree is that which has a stalk. Ibn 'Abbas recited the verse of Safwan ibn Asad al-Tamimi:

"The great plain has made its thorn-trees star-like, and by it the two tribes of Tamim and Wa'il are completed."

Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"Crowned with the roots of the star-like plants, which the south wind weaves, for the tender ones of its water are sheltered."

The derivation of "najm" is from "najama al-shay'" (with damma), "yanjumu nujuman," meaning it appeared and rose. Their prostration is the prostration of their shadows, said by al-Dahhak. al-Farra' said: their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then they incline with it until the shade is shifted. al-Zajjaj said: their prostration is the rotation of the shadow with them, as He said: "whose shadows turn about" (16:48). al-Hasan and Mujahid said: "al-najm" is the star of the sky, and its prostration, according to Mujahid, is the rotation of its shadow, which is the view chosen by al-Tabari, related by al-Mahdawi. It was also said: the prostration of the star is its setting, and the prostration of the tree is the possibility of picking its fruit, related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: all of that is subjected to Allah, so do not worship the star as some of the Sabians worshipped the stars, and many non-Arabs worshipped trees. Prostration is submission, and what is meant by it is the signs of createdness, related by al-Qushayri. al-Nahhas said: the original meaning of prostration in the language is surrender and submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus, among inanimate things it is their surrender to the command of Allah and their submission to Him, and among animals likewise, and it may also be the prostration of prayer. Muhammad ibn Yazid recited, regarding "najm" meaning "nujum," the words of al-Ra'i:

"So she began counting the stars in a cave, swift in the hands of those who eat, their stiffness..."

"And the heaven—He raised it": Abu al-Sammal recited "wa-al-sama'" with a damma, as a beginning (nominative), and he chose this because it is conjoined to the clause "and the star and the tree prostrate," so he made the conjoined element consist of a subject and predicate like the conjoined-to clause. The rest read it with a fatha, governed by an implied verb indicated by what follows.

"And He set up the balance": that is, justice, according to Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi, meaning He set in the earth the justice which He commanded. One says: "Allah set down the Sharia," and "so-and-so set down such-and-such," meaning he threw it. It was also said: on this view the balance is the Qur'an, because in it is the clarification of what is needed; this is the saying of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. al-Hasan, Qatada also, and al-Dahhak said: it is the balance with a tongue by which things are weighed so that people may be given justice from one another, and this is a report with the meaning of a command to justice, indicated by His saying: "And establish the weight with justice" (55:9), and "qist" is justice. It was also said: it is judgment. It was also said: he meant the setting of the balance on the Day of Judgment to weigh deeds. The origin of "mizan" is "mawzan," and the discussion of it has passed in (al-A'raf) (7:85).

"That you not transgress in the balance": the position of "an" may be in the accusative, on the supposition that the preposition is omitted, as if he said: "lest you transgress," like His saying: "Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray" (4:176). It may also be that "an" has no grammatical position, so it means "i.e." and "tatghaw" in this case is jussive, like His saying: "And the chiefs among them went off saying, 'Walk on'" (38:6), meaning "i.e., walk." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice; whoever says it is the instrument by which things are weighed says its transgression is shortchanging. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, do not betray those for whom you weigh. He also said: "O assembly of clients! You have been given charge of two matters by which people were destroyed: the measure and the balance." Whoever says it is judgment says its transgression is distortion. It was also said: there is an implied element here, meaning He set the balance and commanded you not to transgress in it.

"And establish the weight with justice": that is, do it upright with justice. Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Set up the tongue of the balance with justice and fairness." Ibn 'Uyayna said: the establishing is by the hand and the justice is by the heart. Mujahid said: "al-qist" is justice in Roman (Greek) language. It was also said: it is like your saying "he established the prayer," meaning he performed it at its time, and "the people established their markets," meaning they came to them at their time; meaning, do not abandon dealing by weighing with justice.

"And do not make the balance deficient": do not diminish the balance, nor shortchange the measure and the weight. This is like His saying: "And do not diminish the measure and the balance" (11:85). Qatada said regarding this verse: Be just, son of Adam, as you love to be dealt justly with, and fulfil as you love to be fulfilled for you, for justice is the welfare of people. It was also said: the meaning is "do not make deficient the balance of your good deeds on the Day of Resurrection, lest that become a regret for you." The repetition of "the balance" is for the state of the verse-endings. It was also said: the repetition is for the command to give full weight and to observe justice in it. The reading of the common people is "tukhsiru" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the sin. Bilal ibn Abi Burda and Aban from Uthman read "takhsaru" with a fatha on the ta' and the sin, and both are dialects: one says "akhsartu al-mizan" and "khasartuhu," like "ajbartu" and "jabartu." It was also said: "takhsaru," with a fatha on ta' and sin, is taken as implying the omission of the preposition, and the meaning is "and do not be deficient in the balance."

"And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures": "al-anam" means people, according to Ibn 'Abbas. al-Hasan said: the jinn and mankind. al-Dahhak said: everything that crawls on the face of the earth. This is general.

"In it is fruit": that is, everything by which a person enjoys himself of varieties of fruits.

(And the palm-tree, having sheaths)— "al-akmam" is the plural of "kimm" (with a kasra). Al-Jawhari said: al-kimmah (with a kasra), and al-kimamah, is the sheath of the spathe (ṭalʿ) and the covering of the blossom; its plurals are kimam, akimmah, akmam, and also al-akamim. It is said that "kamma al-fasil" when the young camel is cared for, so that it is covered and protected until it grows strong. Al-Ajjaj said:
"Indeed, had you witnessed the people when they were covered, in a stupor, had it not been relieved, they would have been stupefied."
"Tukummu" means they were made to swoon and were covered. "Akammat [[the addition is from al-Jawhari's Sihah]] al-nakhlah" and "kammamat" means it brought forth its sheaths. Al-kimam (with a kasra) and al-kimamah also refer to that which is put over the mouth of a camel so that it does not bite; one says of it: "ba'irun makmum," meaning muzzled. "Kammamtu al-shay'" means I covered the thing. Al-kumm is that which conceals and covers something, and from it is the "kumm" of a shirt (with a damma), its plural being akmam and kimamah, like habb and hibabah. Al-kummah is the round skullcap, because it covers the head. He said:
"I said to them: 'Measure out, with the cap of some of you, your dirhams; indeed I measure out thus.'"

Al-Hasan said: "dhat al-akmam" means "possessing fibre," for the palm is indeed covered with fibre, and its kimam is the fibre that is at its necks. Ibn Zayd said: "possessing spathes before they split open." Ikrimah said: "possessing loads."

(And the grain with its husk, and the sweet-smelling herb)— "al-habb" is wheat, barley and the like. "Al-'asf" is chaff, according to al-Hasan and others. Mujahid said: the leaves of trees and crops. Ibn Abbas said: the straw of the crop and its leaves, which the winds scatter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the green shoots of the crop, that is, what first sprouts from it, and al-Farra' said the same. The Arabs say: "We went out to 'asf the crop," when they cut it before it ripens. Likewise in al-Sihah: "I 'asaftu the crop," meaning I cut it before it ripened. And from Ibn Abbas also: "al-'asf is the leaves of the green crop when its tops are cut and it dries, its parallel being: 'So He made them like a devoured husk' [[see vol. 20 p.]]." Al-Jawhari: "al-zar'" has "a'safa," and "makan mu'sif" means a place abounding in crops. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat al-Ansari said:
"When Jumada withholds its rain, my fields are adorned with a rich, verdant land."
Al-'asf also means earnings, and from it is the saying of the rajiz [[its composer is al-Ajjaj; the verse's first half: "Qad yaksibu al-mal al-hadan al-jafi" (the foolish, coarse man may earn wealth)—"hadan" meaning fool]]:
"Without earnings or acquisition"
And likewise "al-i'tisaf." "Al-'asifah" is the gathered foliage in which the ear of grain is found. Al-Harawi said: "al-'asf" and "al-'asifah" are the leaves of the ear. Al-Tha'labi reported: Ibn al-Sikkit said the Arabs call the leaves of the crop "al-'asf," "al-'asifah," and "al-jill" (with a kasra on the jim). 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah said:
"It waters channels whose 'asifah has inclined, its downward flow from the flowing water is stopped."
In al-Sihah: "al-jill" with a kasra is the stalk of the crop when it is harvested. "Al-rayhan" is provision, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Dahhak said: this is the dialect of Himyar. Also from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah: it is the sweet basil that is smelled, and Ibn Zayd said the same. Also from Ibn Abbas: it is the greenness of the crop. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands upon a stalk. Al-Farra' said: "al-'asf" is the eaten part of the crop, and "al-rayhan" is what is not eaten. Al-Kalbi said: "al-'asf" is the leaf that is not eaten, and "al-rayhan" is the edible grain. It was also said: "al-rayhan" is every fragrant-smelling herb, named so because a person finds a pleasant scent from it, i.e., smells it; so it is fa'lan, rawhan, from "al-ra'ihah" (scent). The root of the yā' in the word is a wāw, changed to yā' to distinguish it from "al-ruhani," which is everything that has a spirit (rūh). Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says "shay' ruhani" and "rayhani," meaning it has a spirit. It may also be on the pattern fay'alan, its root being "rayawhan," the wāw changed to yā' and assimilated, like hayyin and layyin; then lightening was made obligatory because of its length and the addition of the two extra letters, alif and nūn. The basic meaning of the letters rā', wāw and hā' is vibration and movement. In al-Sihah: "al-rayhan" is a well-known plant, and "al-rayhan" is provision; one says: "I went out seeking Allah's rayhan." Al-Nimr ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His rayhan, His mercy and abundant clouds."
In a hadith: "The child is from Allah's rayhan." And their saying "Subhan Allah wa rayhanahu" — they put both in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning glorification of Him and seeking provision. As for His words "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan": al-'asf is the stalk of the crop and al-rayhan its leaves, according to al-Farra'. The reading of the majority, "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan," with the raf' in all of them, is coordinated with "al-fakihah." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and al-Mughirah put all of them in the accusative, coordinated with "al-ard." It was also said: by implying a verb, i.e., "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb," and on this view it is good to pause at "dhat al-akmam." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i put "al-rayhan" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-'asf," meaning: in it is the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb. This is not excluded according to those who understand al-rayhan as provision; it would be as if he said: "and the grain possessing provision." And provision is from the fact that the husk is provision, since the husk is provision for the beasts, and the sweet herb is provision for people. There is no doubt about this for those who say it is the fragrant herb.

His saying, exalted is He: "Fa-bi-ayyi ala'i Rabbikuma tukadhdhiban" (So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?) is addressed to humans and jinn, because "al-anam" applies to both. This is the view of the majority, and it is indicated by the hadith of Jabir mentioned at the beginning of the surah, which al-Tirmidhi narrated, and in it: "The jinn were better than you in response" [[al-Tirmidhi's earlier narration differs in wording from this one; this is al-Hakim's narration]]. It was also said: when He said "He created man" and "He created the jinn," this indicated that what precedes and what follows is for both of them. Also He said: "We shall attend to you, O two burdens" [[al-thaqalan]], which is addressed to humans and jinn, and in this surah He said: "O assembly of jinn and humans." Al-Jurjani said: He addressed the jinn together with the humans even though the jinn were not previously mentioned, as in His saying: "until it was hidden behind the veil" [[see vol. 15 p. 195]]. The jinn were mentioned in what was revealed of the Qur'an earlier, and the Qur'an is like a single surah; so when it is established that they are responsible like humans, the two species are addressed with these verses. It was also said: the address is to humans, according to the Arab custom of addressing one person with the dual form, as previously mentioned regarding "alqiya fi jahannam" [[see p. 16 of this part]]. Likewise the saying:
"Halt, let us weep [[this line opens Imru' al-Qays's mu'allaqah, whose full verse is: "Qifa nabki min dhikra habibin wa manzili bi-saqt al-liwa bayna al-Dakhul fa-Hawmal"]]..."
"O my two companions, halt by Umm Jundab [[the verse opens another qasidah of Imru' al-Qays, and the full verse is: "Khalili marabi ala Umm Jundab, naqdu lubanat al-fu'ad al-mu'adhdhab"]]..."

As for what follows "He created man" and "He created the jinn," it is addressed to both humans and jinn; and the sound view is that of the majority, because of His saying: "And the earth He laid down for the creatures" (al-anam). "Al-ala'" means blessings. This is the view of all the exegetes. Its singular is ila', alan, like mi'a and 'asa, and ilyun and alyun are four dialects, related by al-Nahhas. He said: in the singular of "ana'a al-layl" there are three forms, of which the one with a fatha and an unvowelled lam is dropped; this has been discussed in al-A'raf [[see vol. 7 p. 237]] and al-Najm [[see p. 121 of this part]].

Ibn Zayd said: it means power, and the meaning of the sentence is: "So which power of your Lord will you both deny?" This was also said by al-Kalbi. Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi chose it and said: this surah, among the surahs, is the banner of the Qur'an, and the banner is the commander of the army, which the army follows. It was called a banner only because it is the surah of the attribute of sovereignty and power. He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." So He opened the surah with the name al-Rahman from among the names, so that the servants would know that all that He describes after this of His acts, of His dominion and His power, comes forth to them from the greatest mercy of His being merciful. So He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." Then He mentioned man: "He created man." Then He mentioned what He did to him and what He bestowed upon him. Then He mentioned the reckoning of the sun and the moon, the prostration of things, the stars and trees; He mentioned the raising of the sky, the setting of the balance, which is justice, and the laying down of the earth for the creatures. So He addressed these two weighty ones, the jinn and humans, when they saw what came forth of power and dominion through His mercy, by which He had shown mercy to them, without any benefit or need for it. Yet they associated with Him idols and every object of worship they had taken besides Him, and they denied the mercy by which these things had come forth to them. So He asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? Their denial consisted in their making for Him, in these things which came forth from His dominion and power, a partner who possesses and has power along with Him; that is their denial. Then He mentioned the creation of man from clay, and the creation of the jinn from a smokeless fire, then asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? For He has power in every creation after creation, power after power. So the repetition in these verses is for emphasis and for intensifying the affirmation, and for establishing the proof against them by making them stand before each creation. Al-Qutabi said: God, exalted is He, enumerated in this surah His bounties and mentioned His creation as His favours; then He followed every attribute He described and every blessing He bestowed with this refrain, placing it between each two blessings, to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them, just as you say to one who keeps receiving your kindness yet denies and rejects it: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this? Were you not one who had never performed the pilgrimage (ṣarūrah) and I made the pilgrimage with you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot and I carried you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a context. He said:
"How many a blessing was yours, how many, how many!"
Another said:
"Do not kill a Muslim, if you are a Muslim woman; beware of his blood, beware, beware!"
Another said:
"Do not cut off a friend as long as your eyes weep at the words of a hateful, bitter enemy;
and do not grow weary of visiting him—visit him, visit him, visit him, visit him."
Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: repetition is for driving away heedlessness and for emphasising the proof.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Rahman [Azza wa Jall] is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: except for one verse in it, which is His saying, "Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him" (55:29). It has seventy-six verses. Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said: it is entirely Medinan. The first opinion is more sound, because of what 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr narrated, who said: The first person to recite the Qur'an aloud in Mecca after the Prophet (ﷺ) was Ibn Mas'ud. That was because the Companions said: "Quraysh has never heard this Qur'an recited aloud. Who will make them hear it?" Ibn Mas'ud said: "I will." They said: "We fear for you; we want a man who has a clan to protect him." He refused, then stood at the Station (al-Maqam) and said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an" (55:1–2), and he continued, raising his voice with it, while Quraysh was in its assemblies. They paid attention and said: "What is the son of Umm 'Abd saying?" They said: "He is saying what Muhammad claims was revealed to him." Then they beat him until they left marks on his face.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray the dawn prayer at Nakhla, and recited Surat al-Rahman, and a group of jinn passed by and believed in him. In al-Tirmidhi, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from beginning to end, and they were silent. He said: "I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they were better in response than you. Every time I came to His saying, 'So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?' (55:13), they said: 'No, by nothing of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny; to You is the praise.'" He said: this is a strange (gharib) hadith. In this is evidence that it is Meccan, and Allah knows best. It was also narrated that Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Recite to me of what has been revealed to you." He recited to him Surat al-Rahman. He said: "Repeat it." He repeated it three times. He said: "By Allah, indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a sweetness, its lower part is abundant, its upper part is fruitful, and this is not the speech of a human being. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah."

It was also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For everything there is a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is Surat al-Rahman."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The Most Merciful (1), taught the Qur'an (2), created man (3), taught him eloquence (4).
The sun and the moon run by a reckoning (5), and the star and the tree prostrate (6), and the heaven—He raised it and set up the balance (7), that you not transgress in the balance (8), and establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient (9).
And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures (10), in it is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths (11), and grain with its husk and fragrant plants (12). So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? (13)

His saying, Exalted is He: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Amir al-Sha'bi said: "al-Rahman" is the opening of three surahs which, when combined, form a name of Allah, the Exalted: (Alif-Lam-Ra) and (Ha-Mim) and (Nun), so the combined letters are "al-Rahman."

"Taught the Qur'an": that is, He taught it to His Prophet (ﷺ) until he conveyed it to all people. It was revealed when they said: "And what is the Rahman?" It was also said: it was revealed as a reply to the people of Mecca when they said: "He is only taught by a human being," and "the Rahman of Yamama," meaning Musaylima the Liar. So Allah revealed: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "taught the Qur'an" is that He made it easy to be remembered and recited, as He said: "And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance" (54:17). It was also said: He made it a sign of what people are to worship by.

"Created man": Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan said: it means Adam, peace be upon him.

"Taught him eloquence": the names of everything. It was also said: He taught him all languages. Also from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kaysan: "man" here is intended to mean Muhammad (ﷺ), and "eloquence" is the clarification of the lawful from the unlawful, and of guidance from error. It was also said: what has been and what will be, because he explained about the former and the latter and the Day of Judgment. Al-Dahhak said: "al-Bayan" is good and evil. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is what benefits him and what harms him, and Qatada said the same. It was also said: "man" is intended to mean all people, so it is a generic noun, and "eloquence" on this view is speech and understanding, which is among what man is distinguished by over the rest of the animals. al-Suddi said: He taught every people their tongue with which they speak. Yaman said: writing and inscription with the pen, like His saying: "He who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know" (96:4–5).

"The sun and the moon run by a reckoning": that is, they run according to a known computation, so the predicate is omitted. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu Malik said: that is, they run by a reckoning, in mansions which they do not exceed and from which they do not deviate. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kaysan said: it means that by them time and the terms of lives are reckoned, and were it not for the night, the day, the sun and the moon, no one would know how to count anything, even if the whole age were day. al-Suddi said: "bi-husban" is the determination of their terms, meaning they run for terms like the terms of people, so when their term comes they perish. A similar expression is: "Each runs to a specified term" (13:2 / 31:29 / 39:5). al-Dahhak said: "by a measure." Mujahid said: "bi-husban" is like the husban of a millstone, meaning its pivot, they revolve around it like a pivot. Al-husban may be a verbal noun of "hasabtuhu uhsibuhu" (with damma), husban and husbanan, like al-ghufran, al-kufran and al-rujhan, and also "hisaba," meaning I counted it. al-Akhfash said: it may also be the plural of hisab, like shihab and shuhban. Al-husban also means punishment and short arrows, and it has passed in (al-Kahf) (18:40); its singular is husbana. Al-husbana also means a small cushion. From it one says: "hasabtuhu" when I placed a cushion for him, and a poet said:

"...you would have reclined, not cushioned"

meaning not placed on a cushion, meaning not honoured nor shrouded.

"And the star and the tree prostrate": Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the star is that which has no stalk, and the tree is that which has a stalk. Ibn 'Abbas recited the verse of Safwan ibn Asad al-Tamimi:

"The great plain has made its thorn-trees star-like, and by it the two tribes of Tamim and Wa'il are completed."

Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"Crowned with the roots of the star-like plants, which the south wind weaves, for the tender ones of its water are sheltered."

The derivation of "najm" is from "najama al-shay'" (with damma), "yanjumu nujuman," meaning it appeared and rose. Their prostration is the prostration of their shadows, said by al-Dahhak. al-Farra' said: their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then they incline with it until the shade is shifted. al-Zajjaj said: their prostration is the rotation of the shadow with them, as He said: "whose shadows turn about" (16:48). al-Hasan and Mujahid said: "al-najm" is the star of the sky, and its prostration, according to Mujahid, is the rotation of its shadow, which is the view chosen by al-Tabari, related by al-Mahdawi. It was also said: the prostration of the star is its setting, and the prostration of the tree is the possibility of picking its fruit, related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: all of that is subjected to Allah, so do not worship the star as some of the Sabians worshipped the stars, and many non-Arabs worshipped trees. Prostration is submission, and what is meant by it is the signs of createdness, related by al-Qushayri. al-Nahhas said: the original meaning of prostration in the language is surrender and submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus, among inanimate things it is their surrender to the command of Allah and their submission to Him, and among animals likewise, and it may also be the prostration of prayer. Muhammad ibn Yazid recited, regarding "najm" meaning "nujum," the words of al-Ra'i:

"So she began counting the stars in a cave, swift in the hands of those who eat, their stiffness..."

"And the heaven—He raised it": Abu al-Sammal recited "wa-al-sama'" with a damma, as a beginning (nominative), and he chose this because it is conjoined to the clause "and the star and the tree prostrate," so he made the conjoined element consist of a subject and predicate like the conjoined-to clause. The rest read it with a fatha, governed by an implied verb indicated by what follows.

"And He set up the balance": that is, justice, according to Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi, meaning He set in the earth the justice which He commanded. One says: "Allah set down the Sharia," and "so-and-so set down such-and-such," meaning he threw it. It was also said: on this view the balance is the Qur'an, because in it is the clarification of what is needed; this is the saying of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. al-Hasan, Qatada also, and al-Dahhak said: it is the balance with a tongue by which things are weighed so that people may be given justice from one another, and this is a report with the meaning of a command to justice, indicated by His saying: "And establish the weight with justice" (55:9), and "qist" is justice. It was also said: it is judgment. It was also said: he meant the setting of the balance on the Day of Judgment to weigh deeds. The origin of "mizan" is "mawzan," and the discussion of it has passed in (al-A'raf) (7:85).

"That you not transgress in the balance": the position of "an" may be in the accusative, on the supposition that the preposition is omitted, as if he said: "lest you transgress," like His saying: "Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray" (4:176). It may also be that "an" has no grammatical position, so it means "i.e." and "tatghaw" in this case is jussive, like His saying: "And the chiefs among them went off saying, 'Walk on'" (38:6), meaning "i.e., walk." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice; whoever says it is the instrument by which things are weighed says its transgression is shortchanging. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, do not betray those for whom you weigh. He also said: "O assembly of clients! You have been given charge of two matters by which people were destroyed: the measure and the balance." Whoever says it is judgment says its transgression is distortion. It was also said: there is an implied element here, meaning He set the balance and commanded you not to transgress in it.

"And establish the weight with justice": that is, do it upright with justice. Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Set up the tongue of the balance with justice and fairness." Ibn 'Uyayna said: the establishing is by the hand and the justice is by the heart. Mujahid said: "al-qist" is justice in Roman (Greek) language. It was also said: it is like your saying "he established the prayer," meaning he performed it at its time, and "the people established their markets," meaning they came to them at their time; meaning, do not abandon dealing by weighing with justice.

"And do not make the balance deficient": do not diminish the balance, nor shortchange the measure and the weight. This is like His saying: "And do not diminish the measure and the balance" (11:85). Qatada said regarding this verse: Be just, son of Adam, as you love to be dealt justly with, and fulfil as you love to be fulfilled for you, for justice is the welfare of people. It was also said: the meaning is "do not make deficient the balance of your good deeds on the Day of Resurrection, lest that become a regret for you." The repetition of "the balance" is for the state of the verse-endings. It was also said: the repetition is for the command to give full weight and to observe justice in it. The reading of the common people is "tukhsiru" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the sin. Bilal ibn Abi Burda and Aban from Uthman read "takhsaru" with a fatha on the ta' and the sin, and both are dialects: one says "akhsartu al-mizan" and "khasartuhu," like "ajbartu" and "jabartu." It was also said: "takhsaru," with a fatha on ta' and sin, is taken as implying the omission of the preposition, and the meaning is "and do not be deficient in the balance."

"And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures": "al-anam" means people, according to Ibn 'Abbas. al-Hasan said: the jinn and mankind. al-Dahhak said: everything that crawls on the face of the earth. This is general.

"In it is fruit": that is, everything by which a person enjoys himself of varieties of fruits.

(And the palm-tree, having sheaths)— "al-akmam" is the plural of "kimm" (with a kasra). Al-Jawhari said: al-kimmah (with a kasra), and al-kimamah, is the sheath of the spathe (ṭalʿ) and the covering of the blossom; its plurals are kimam, akimmah, akmam, and also al-akamim. It is said that "kamma al-fasil" when the young camel is cared for, so that it is covered and protected until it grows strong. Al-Ajjaj said:
"Indeed, had you witnessed the people when they were covered, in a stupor, had it not been relieved, they would have been stupefied."
"Tukummu" means they were made to swoon and were covered. "Akammat [[the addition is from al-Jawhari's Sihah]] al-nakhlah" and "kammamat" means it brought forth its sheaths. Al-kimam (with a kasra) and al-kimamah also refer to that which is put over the mouth of a camel so that it does not bite; one says of it: "ba'irun makmum," meaning muzzled. "Kammamtu al-shay'" means I covered the thing. Al-kumm is that which conceals and covers something, and from it is the "kumm" of a shirt (with a damma), its plural being akmam and kimamah, like habb and hibabah. Al-kummah is the round skullcap, because it covers the head. He said:
"I said to them: 'Measure out, with the cap of some of you, your dirhams; indeed I measure out thus.'"

Al-Hasan said: "dhat al-akmam" means "possessing fibre," for the palm is indeed covered with fibre, and its kimam is the fibre that is at its necks. Ibn Zayd said: "possessing spathes before they split open." Ikrimah said: "possessing loads."

(And the grain with its husk, and the sweet-smelling herb)— "al-habb" is wheat, barley and the like. "Al-'asf" is chaff, according to al-Hasan and others. Mujahid said: the leaves of trees and crops. Ibn Abbas said: the straw of the crop and its leaves, which the winds scatter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the green shoots of the crop, that is, what first sprouts from it, and al-Farra' said the same. The Arabs say: "We went out to 'asf the crop," when they cut it before it ripens. Likewise in al-Sihah: "I 'asaftu the crop," meaning I cut it before it ripened. And from Ibn Abbas also: "al-'asf is the leaves of the green crop when its tops are cut and it dries, its parallel being: 'So He made them like a devoured husk' [[see vol. 20 p.]]." Al-Jawhari: "al-zar'" has "a'safa," and "makan mu'sif" means a place abounding in crops. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat al-Ansari said:
"When Jumada withholds its rain, my fields are adorned with a rich, verdant land."
Al-'asf also means earnings, and from it is the saying of the rajiz [[its composer is al-Ajjaj; the verse's first half: "Qad yaksibu al-mal al-hadan al-jafi" (the foolish, coarse man may earn wealth)—"hadan" meaning fool]]:
"Without earnings or acquisition"
And likewise "al-i'tisaf." "Al-'asifah" is the gathered foliage in which the ear of grain is found. Al-Harawi said: "al-'asf" and "al-'asifah" are the leaves of the ear. Al-Tha'labi reported: Ibn al-Sikkit said the Arabs call the leaves of the crop "al-'asf," "al-'asifah," and "al-jill" (with a kasra on the jim). 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah said:
"It waters channels whose 'asifah has inclined, its downward flow from the flowing water is stopped."
In al-Sihah: "al-jill" with a kasra is the stalk of the crop when it is harvested. "Al-rayhan" is provision, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Dahhak said: this is the dialect of Himyar. Also from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah: it is the sweet basil that is smelled, and Ibn Zayd said the same. Also from Ibn Abbas: it is the greenness of the crop. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands upon a stalk. Al-Farra' said: "al-'asf" is the eaten part of the crop, and "al-rayhan" is what is not eaten. Al-Kalbi said: "al-'asf" is the leaf that is not eaten, and "al-rayhan" is the edible grain. It was also said: "al-rayhan" is every fragrant-smelling herb, named so because a person finds a pleasant scent from it, i.e., smells it; so it is fa'lan, rawhan, from "al-ra'ihah" (scent). The root of the yā' in the word is a wāw, changed to yā' to distinguish it from "al-ruhani," which is everything that has a spirit (rūh). Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says "shay' ruhani" and "rayhani," meaning it has a spirit. It may also be on the pattern fay'alan, its root being "rayawhan," the wāw changed to yā' and assimilated, like hayyin and layyin; then lightening was made obligatory because of its length and the addition of the two extra letters, alif and nūn. The basic meaning of the letters rā', wāw and hā' is vibration and movement. In al-Sihah: "al-rayhan" is a well-known plant, and "al-rayhan" is provision; one says: "I went out seeking Allah's rayhan." Al-Nimr ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His rayhan, His mercy and abundant clouds."
In a hadith: "The child is from Allah's rayhan." And their saying "Subhan Allah wa rayhanahu" — they put both in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning glorification of Him and seeking provision. As for His words "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan": al-'asf is the stalk of the crop and al-rayhan its leaves, according to al-Farra'. The reading of the majority, "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan," with the raf' in all of them, is coordinated with "al-fakihah." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and al-Mughirah put all of them in the accusative, coordinated with "al-ard." It was also said: by implying a verb, i.e., "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb," and on this view it is good to pause at "dhat al-akmam." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i put "al-rayhan" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-'asf," meaning: in it is the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb. This is not excluded according to those who understand al-rayhan as provision; it would be as if he said: "and the grain possessing provision." And provision is from the fact that the husk is provision, since the husk is provision for the beasts, and the sweet herb is provision for people. There is no doubt about this for those who say it is the fragrant herb.

His saying, exalted is He: "Fa-bi-ayyi ala'i Rabbikuma tukadhdhiban" (So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?) is addressed to humans and jinn, because "al-anam" applies to both. This is the view of the majority, and it is indicated by the hadith of Jabir mentioned at the beginning of the surah, which al-Tirmidhi narrated, and in it: "The jinn were better than you in response" [[al-Tirmidhi's earlier narration differs in wording from this one; this is al-Hakim's narration]]. It was also said: when He said "He created man" and "He created the jinn," this indicated that what precedes and what follows is for both of them. Also He said: "We shall attend to you, O two burdens" [[al-thaqalan]], which is addressed to humans and jinn, and in this surah He said: "O assembly of jinn and humans." Al-Jurjani said: He addressed the jinn together with the humans even though the jinn were not previously mentioned, as in His saying: "until it was hidden behind the veil" [[see vol. 15 p. 195]]. The jinn were mentioned in what was revealed of the Qur'an earlier, and the Qur'an is like a single surah; so when it is established that they are responsible like humans, the two species are addressed with these verses. It was also said: the address is to humans, according to the Arab custom of addressing one person with the dual form, as previously mentioned regarding "alqiya fi jahannam" [[see p. 16 of this part]]. Likewise the saying:
"Halt, let us weep [[this line opens Imru' al-Qays's mu'allaqah, whose full verse is: "Qifa nabki min dhikra habibin wa manzili bi-saqt al-liwa bayna al-Dakhul fa-Hawmal"]]..."
"O my two companions, halt by Umm Jundab [[the verse opens another qasidah of Imru' al-Qays, and the full verse is: "Khalili marabi ala Umm Jundab, naqdu lubanat al-fu'ad al-mu'adhdhab"]]..."

As for what follows "He created man" and "He created the jinn," it is addressed to both humans and jinn; and the sound view is that of the majority, because of His saying: "And the earth He laid down for the creatures" (al-anam). "Al-ala'" means blessings. This is the view of all the exegetes. Its singular is ila', alan, like mi'a and 'asa, and ilyun and alyun are four dialects, related by al-Nahhas. He said: in the singular of "ana'a al-layl" there are three forms, of which the one with a fatha and an unvowelled lam is dropped; this has been discussed in al-A'raf [[see vol. 7 p. 237]] and al-Najm [[see p. 121 of this part]].

Ibn Zayd said: it means power, and the meaning of the sentence is: "So which power of your Lord will you both deny?" This was also said by al-Kalbi. Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi chose it and said: this surah, among the surahs, is the banner of the Qur'an, and the banner is the commander of the army, which the army follows. It was called a banner only because it is the surah of the attribute of sovereignty and power. He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." So He opened the surah with the name al-Rahman from among the names, so that the servants would know that all that He describes after this of His acts, of His dominion and His power, comes forth to them from the greatest mercy of His being merciful. So He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." Then He mentioned man: "He created man." Then He mentioned what He did to him and what He bestowed upon him. Then He mentioned the reckoning of the sun and the moon, the prostration of things, the stars and trees; He mentioned the raising of the sky, the setting of the balance, which is justice, and the laying down of the earth for the creatures. So He addressed these two weighty ones, the jinn and humans, when they saw what came forth of power and dominion through His mercy, by which He had shown mercy to them, without any benefit or need for it. Yet they associated with Him idols and every object of worship they had taken besides Him, and they denied the mercy by which these things had come forth to them. So He asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? Their denial consisted in their making for Him, in these things which came forth from His dominion and power, a partner who possesses and has power along with Him; that is their denial. Then He mentioned the creation of man from clay, and the creation of the jinn from a smokeless fire, then asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? For He has power in every creation after creation, power after power. So the repetition in these verses is for emphasis and for intensifying the affirmation, and for establishing the proof against them by making them stand before each creation. Al-Qutabi said: God, exalted is He, enumerated in this surah His bounties and mentioned His creation as His favours; then He followed every attribute He described and every blessing He bestowed with this refrain, placing it between each two blessings, to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them, just as you say to one who keeps receiving your kindness yet denies and rejects it: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this? Were you not one who had never performed the pilgrimage (ṣarūrah) and I made the pilgrimage with you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot and I carried you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a context. He said:
"How many a blessing was yours, how many, how many!"
Another said:
"Do not kill a Muslim, if you are a Muslim woman; beware of his blood, beware, beware!"
Another said:
"Do not cut off a friend as long as your eyes weep at the words of a hateful, bitter enemy;
and do not grow weary of visiting him—visit him, visit him, visit him, visit him."
Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: repetition is for driving away heedlessness and for emphasising the proof.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Rahman [Azza wa Jall] is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: except for one verse in it, which is His saying, "Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him" (55:29). It has seventy-six verses. Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said: it is entirely Medinan. The first opinion is more sound, because of what 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr narrated, who said: The first person to recite the Qur'an aloud in Mecca after the Prophet (ﷺ) was Ibn Mas'ud. That was because the Companions said: "Quraysh has never heard this Qur'an recited aloud. Who will make them hear it?" Ibn Mas'ud said: "I will." They said: "We fear for you; we want a man who has a clan to protect him." He refused, then stood at the Station (al-Maqam) and said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an" (55:1–2), and he continued, raising his voice with it, while Quraysh was in its assemblies. They paid attention and said: "What is the son of Umm 'Abd saying?" They said: "He is saying what Muhammad claims was revealed to him." Then they beat him until they left marks on his face.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray the dawn prayer at Nakhla, and recited Surat al-Rahman, and a group of jinn passed by and believed in him. In al-Tirmidhi, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from beginning to end, and they were silent. He said: "I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they were better in response than you. Every time I came to His saying, 'So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?' (55:13), they said: 'No, by nothing of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny; to You is the praise.'" He said: this is a strange (gharib) hadith. In this is evidence that it is Meccan, and Allah knows best. It was also narrated that Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Recite to me of what has been revealed to you." He recited to him Surat al-Rahman. He said: "Repeat it." He repeated it three times. He said: "By Allah, indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a sweetness, its lower part is abundant, its upper part is fruitful, and this is not the speech of a human being. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah."

It was also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For everything there is a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is Surat al-Rahman."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The Most Merciful (1), taught the Qur'an (2), created man (3), taught him eloquence (4).
The sun and the moon run by a reckoning (5), and the star and the tree prostrate (6), and the heaven—He raised it and set up the balance (7), that you not transgress in the balance (8), and establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient (9).
And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures (10), in it is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths (11), and grain with its husk and fragrant plants (12). So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? (13)

His saying, Exalted is He: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Amir al-Sha'bi said: "al-Rahman" is the opening of three surahs which, when combined, form a name of Allah, the Exalted: (Alif-Lam-Ra) and (Ha-Mim) and (Nun), so the combined letters are "al-Rahman."

"Taught the Qur'an": that is, He taught it to His Prophet (ﷺ) until he conveyed it to all people. It was revealed when they said: "And what is the Rahman?" It was also said: it was revealed as a reply to the people of Mecca when they said: "He is only taught by a human being," and "the Rahman of Yamama," meaning Musaylima the Liar. So Allah revealed: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "taught the Qur'an" is that He made it easy to be remembered and recited, as He said: "And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance" (54:17). It was also said: He made it a sign of what people are to worship by.

"Created man": Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan said: it means Adam, peace be upon him.

"Taught him eloquence": the names of everything. It was also said: He taught him all languages. Also from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kaysan: "man" here is intended to mean Muhammad (ﷺ), and "eloquence" is the clarification of the lawful from the unlawful, and of guidance from error. It was also said: what has been and what will be, because he explained about the former and the latter and the Day of Judgment. Al-Dahhak said: "al-Bayan" is good and evil. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is what benefits him and what harms him, and Qatada said the same. It was also said: "man" is intended to mean all people, so it is a generic noun, and "eloquence" on this view is speech and understanding, which is among what man is distinguished by over the rest of the animals. al-Suddi said: He taught every people their tongue with which they speak. Yaman said: writing and inscription with the pen, like His saying: "He who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know" (96:4–5).

"The sun and the moon run by a reckoning": that is, they run according to a known computation, so the predicate is omitted. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu Malik said: that is, they run by a reckoning, in mansions which they do not exceed and from which they do not deviate. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kaysan said: it means that by them time and the terms of lives are reckoned, and were it not for the night, the day, the sun and the moon, no one would know how to count anything, even if the whole age were day. al-Suddi said: "bi-husban" is the determination of their terms, meaning they run for terms like the terms of people, so when their term comes they perish. A similar expression is: "Each runs to a specified term" (13:2 / 31:29 / 39:5). al-Dahhak said: "by a measure." Mujahid said: "bi-husban" is like the husban of a millstone, meaning its pivot, they revolve around it like a pivot. Al-husban may be a verbal noun of "hasabtuhu uhsibuhu" (with damma), husban and husbanan, like al-ghufran, al-kufran and al-rujhan, and also "hisaba," meaning I counted it. al-Akhfash said: it may also be the plural of hisab, like shihab and shuhban. Al-husban also means punishment and short arrows, and it has passed in (al-Kahf) (18:40); its singular is husbana. Al-husbana also means a small cushion. From it one says: "hasabtuhu" when I placed a cushion for him, and a poet said:

"...you would have reclined, not cushioned"

meaning not placed on a cushion, meaning not honoured nor shrouded.

"And the star and the tree prostrate": Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the star is that which has no stalk, and the tree is that which has a stalk. Ibn 'Abbas recited the verse of Safwan ibn Asad al-Tamimi:

"The great plain has made its thorn-trees star-like, and by it the two tribes of Tamim and Wa'il are completed."

Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"Crowned with the roots of the star-like plants, which the south wind weaves, for the tender ones of its water are sheltered."

The derivation of "najm" is from "najama al-shay'" (with damma), "yanjumu nujuman," meaning it appeared and rose. Their prostration is the prostration of their shadows, said by al-Dahhak. al-Farra' said: their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then they incline with it until the shade is shifted. al-Zajjaj said: their prostration is the rotation of the shadow with them, as He said: "whose shadows turn about" (16:48). al-Hasan and Mujahid said: "al-najm" is the star of the sky, and its prostration, according to Mujahid, is the rotation of its shadow, which is the view chosen by al-Tabari, related by al-Mahdawi. It was also said: the prostration of the star is its setting, and the prostration of the tree is the possibility of picking its fruit, related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: all of that is subjected to Allah, so do not worship the star as some of the Sabians worshipped the stars, and many non-Arabs worshipped trees. Prostration is submission, and what is meant by it is the signs of createdness, related by al-Qushayri. al-Nahhas said: the original meaning of prostration in the language is surrender and submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Thus, among inanimate things it is their surrender to the command of Allah and their submission to Him, and among animals likewise, and it may also be the prostration of prayer. Muhammad ibn Yazid recited, regarding "najm" meaning "nujum," the words of al-Ra'i:

"So she began counting the stars in a cave, swift in the hands of those who eat, their stiffness..."

"And the heaven—He raised it": Abu al-Sammal recited "wa-al-sama'" with a damma, as a beginning (nominative), and he chose this because it is conjoined to the clause "and the star and the tree prostrate," so he made the conjoined element consist of a subject and predicate like the conjoined-to clause. The rest read it with a fatha, governed by an implied verb indicated by what follows.

"And He set up the balance": that is, justice, according to Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi, meaning He set in the earth the justice which He commanded. One says: "Allah set down the Sharia," and "so-and-so set down such-and-such," meaning he threw it. It was also said: on this view the balance is the Qur'an, because in it is the clarification of what is needed; this is the saying of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. al-Hasan, Qatada also, and al-Dahhak said: it is the balance with a tongue by which things are weighed so that people may be given justice from one another, and this is a report with the meaning of a command to justice, indicated by His saying: "And establish the weight with justice" (55:9), and "qist" is justice. It was also said: it is judgment. It was also said: he meant the setting of the balance on the Day of Judgment to weigh deeds. The origin of "mizan" is "mawzan," and the discussion of it has passed in (al-A'raf) (7:85).

"That you not transgress in the balance": the position of "an" may be in the accusative, on the supposition that the preposition is omitted, as if he said: "lest you transgress," like His saying: "Allah makes clear to you lest you go astray" (4:176). It may also be that "an" has no grammatical position, so it means "i.e." and "tatghaw" in this case is jussive, like His saying: "And the chiefs among them went off saying, 'Walk on'" (38:6), meaning "i.e., walk." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice; whoever says it is the instrument by which things are weighed says its transgression is shortchanging. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, do not betray those for whom you weigh. He also said: "O assembly of clients! You have been given charge of two matters by which people were destroyed: the measure and the balance." Whoever says it is judgment says its transgression is distortion. It was also said: there is an implied element here, meaning He set the balance and commanded you not to transgress in it.

"And establish the weight with justice": that is, do it upright with justice. Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Set up the tongue of the balance with justice and fairness." Ibn 'Uyayna said: the establishing is by the hand and the justice is by the heart. Mujahid said: "al-qist" is justice in Roman (Greek) language. It was also said: it is like your saying "he established the prayer," meaning he performed it at its time, and "the people established their markets," meaning they came to them at their time; meaning, do not abandon dealing by weighing with justice.

"And do not make the balance deficient": do not diminish the balance, nor shortchange the measure and the weight. This is like His saying: "And do not diminish the measure and the balance" (11:85). Qatada said regarding this verse: Be just, son of Adam, as you love to be dealt justly with, and fulfil as you love to be fulfilled for you, for justice is the welfare of people. It was also said: the meaning is "do not make deficient the balance of your good deeds on the Day of Resurrection, lest that become a regret for you." The repetition of "the balance" is for the state of the verse-endings. It was also said: the repetition is for the command to give full weight and to observe justice in it. The reading of the common people is "tukhsiru" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the sin. Bilal ibn Abi Burda and Aban from Uthman read "takhsaru" with a fatha on the ta' and the sin, and both are dialects: one says "akhsartu al-mizan" and "khasartuhu," like "ajbartu" and "jabartu." It was also said: "takhsaru," with a fatha on ta' and sin, is taken as implying the omission of the preposition, and the meaning is "and do not be deficient in the balance."

"And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures": "al-anam" means people, according to Ibn 'Abbas. al-Hasan said: the jinn and mankind. al-Dahhak said: everything that crawls on the face of the earth. This is general.

"In it is fruit": that is, everything by which a person enjoys himself of varieties of fruits.

(And the palm-tree, having sheaths)— "al-akmam" is the plural of "kimm" (with a kasra). Al-Jawhari said: al-kimmah (with a kasra), and al-kimamah, is the sheath of the spathe (ṭalʿ) and the covering of the blossom; its plurals are kimam, akimmah, akmam, and also al-akamim. It is said that "kamma al-fasil" when the young camel is cared for, so that it is covered and protected until it grows strong. Al-Ajjaj said:
"Indeed, had you witnessed the people when they were covered, in a stupor, had it not been relieved, they would have been stupefied."
"Tukummu" means they were made to swoon and were covered. "Akammat [[the addition is from al-Jawhari's Sihah]] al-nakhlah" and "kammamat" means it brought forth its sheaths. Al-kimam (with a kasra) and al-kimamah also refer to that which is put over the mouth of a camel so that it does not bite; one says of it: "ba'irun makmum," meaning muzzled. "Kammamtu al-shay'" means I covered the thing. Al-kumm is that which conceals and covers something, and from it is the "kumm" of a shirt (with a damma), its plural being akmam and kimamah, like habb and hibabah. Al-kummah is the round skullcap, because it covers the head. He said:
"I said to them: 'Measure out, with the cap of some of you, your dirhams; indeed I measure out thus.'"

Al-Hasan said: "dhat al-akmam" means "possessing fibre," for the palm is indeed covered with fibre, and its kimam is the fibre that is at its necks. Ibn Zayd said: "possessing spathes before they split open." Ikrimah said: "possessing loads."

(And the grain with its husk, and the sweet-smelling herb)— "al-habb" is wheat, barley and the like. "Al-'asf" is chaff, according to al-Hasan and others. Mujahid said: the leaves of trees and crops. Ibn Abbas said: the straw of the crop and its leaves, which the winds scatter. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the green shoots of the crop, that is, what first sprouts from it, and al-Farra' said the same. The Arabs say: "We went out to 'asf the crop," when they cut it before it ripens. Likewise in al-Sihah: "I 'asaftu the crop," meaning I cut it before it ripened. And from Ibn Abbas also: "al-'asf is the leaves of the green crop when its tops are cut and it dries, its parallel being: 'So He made them like a devoured husk' [[see vol. 20 p.]]." Al-Jawhari: "al-zar'" has "a'safa," and "makan mu'sif" means a place abounding in crops. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat al-Ansari said:
"When Jumada withholds its rain, my fields are adorned with a rich, verdant land."
Al-'asf also means earnings, and from it is the saying of the rajiz [[its composer is al-Ajjaj; the verse's first half: "Qad yaksibu al-mal al-hadan al-jafi" (the foolish, coarse man may earn wealth)—"hadan" meaning fool]]:
"Without earnings or acquisition"
And likewise "al-i'tisaf." "Al-'asifah" is the gathered foliage in which the ear of grain is found. Al-Harawi said: "al-'asf" and "al-'asifah" are the leaves of the ear. Al-Tha'labi reported: Ibn al-Sikkit said the Arabs call the leaves of the crop "al-'asf," "al-'asifah," and "al-jill" (with a kasra on the jim). 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah said:
"It waters channels whose 'asifah has inclined, its downward flow from the flowing water is stopped."
In al-Sihah: "al-jill" with a kasra is the stalk of the crop when it is harvested. "Al-rayhan" is provision, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Dahhak said: this is the dialect of Himyar. Also from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah: it is the sweet basil that is smelled, and Ibn Zayd said the same. Also from Ibn Abbas: it is the greenness of the crop. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands upon a stalk. Al-Farra' said: "al-'asf" is the eaten part of the crop, and "al-rayhan" is what is not eaten. Al-Kalbi said: "al-'asf" is the leaf that is not eaten, and "al-rayhan" is the edible grain. It was also said: "al-rayhan" is every fragrant-smelling herb, named so because a person finds a pleasant scent from it, i.e., smells it; so it is fa'lan, rawhan, from "al-ra'ihah" (scent). The root of the yā' in the word is a wāw, changed to yā' to distinguish it from "al-ruhani," which is everything that has a spirit (rūh). Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says "shay' ruhani" and "rayhani," meaning it has a spirit. It may also be on the pattern fay'alan, its root being "rayawhan," the wāw changed to yā' and assimilated, like hayyin and layyin; then lightening was made obligatory because of its length and the addition of the two extra letters, alif and nūn. The basic meaning of the letters rā', wāw and hā' is vibration and movement. In al-Sihah: "al-rayhan" is a well-known plant, and "al-rayhan" is provision; one says: "I went out seeking Allah's rayhan." Al-Nimr ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His rayhan, His mercy and abundant clouds."
In a hadith: "The child is from Allah's rayhan." And their saying "Subhan Allah wa rayhanahu" — they put both in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning glorification of Him and seeking provision. As for His words "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan": al-'asf is the stalk of the crop and al-rayhan its leaves, according to al-Farra'. The reading of the majority, "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan," with the raf' in all of them, is coordinated with "al-fakihah." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and al-Mughirah put all of them in the accusative, coordinated with "al-ard." It was also said: by implying a verb, i.e., "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb," and on this view it is good to pause at "dhat al-akmam." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i put "al-rayhan" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-'asf," meaning: in it is the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb. This is not excluded according to those who understand al-rayhan as provision; it would be as if he said: "and the grain possessing provision." And provision is from the fact that the husk is provision, since the husk is provision for the beasts, and the sweet herb is provision for people. There is no doubt about this for those who say it is the fragrant herb.

His saying, exalted is He: "Fa-bi-ayyi ala'i Rabbikuma tukadhdhiban" (So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?) is addressed to humans and jinn, because "al-anam" applies to both. This is the view of the majority, and it is indicated by the hadith of Jabir mentioned at the beginning of the surah, which al-Tirmidhi narrated, and in it: "The jinn were better than you in response" [[al-Tirmidhi's earlier narration differs in wording from this one; this is al-Hakim's narration]]. It was also said: when He said "He created man" and "He created the jinn," this indicated that what precedes and what follows is for both of them. Also He said: "We shall attend to you, O two burdens" [[al-thaqalan]], which is addressed to humans and jinn, and in this surah He said: "O assembly of jinn and humans." Al-Jurjani said: He addressed the jinn together with the humans even though the jinn were not previously mentioned, as in His saying: "until it was hidden behind the veil" [[see vol. 15 p. 195]]. The jinn were mentioned in what was revealed of the Qur'an earlier, and the Qur'an is like a single surah; so when it is established that they are responsible like humans, the two species are addressed with these verses. It was also said: the address is to humans, according to the Arab custom of addressing one person with the dual form, as previously mentioned regarding "alqiya fi jahannam" [[see p. 16 of this part]]. Likewise the saying:
"Halt, let us weep [[this line opens Imru' al-Qays's mu'allaqah, whose full verse is: "Qifa nabki min dhikra habibin wa manzili bi-saqt al-liwa bayna al-Dakhul fa-Hawmal"]]..."
"O my two companions, halt by Umm Jundab [[the verse opens another qasidah of Imru' al-Qays, and the full verse is: "Khalili marabi ala Umm Jundab, naqdu lubanat al-fu'ad al-mu'adhdhab"]]..."

As for what follows "He created man" and "He created the jinn," it is addressed to both humans and jinn; and the sound view is that of the majority, because of His saying: "And the earth He laid down for the creatures" (al-anam). "Al-ala'" means blessings. This is the view of all the exegetes. Its singular is ila', alan, like mi'a and 'asa, and ilyun and alyun are four dialects, related by al-Nahhas. He said: in the singular of "ana'a al-layl" there are three forms, of which the one with a fatha and an unvowelled lam is dropped; this has been discussed in al-A'raf [[see vol. 7 p. 237]] and al-Najm [[see p. 121 of this part]].

Ibn Zayd said: it means power, and the meaning of the sentence is: "So which power of your Lord will you both deny?" This was also said by al-Kalbi. Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi chose it and said: this surah, among the surahs, is the banner of the Qur'an, and the banner is the commander of the army, which the army follows. It was called a banner only because it is the surah of the attribute of sovereignty and power. He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." So He opened the surah with the name al-Rahman from among the names, so that the servants would know that all that He describes after this of His acts, of His dominion and His power, comes forth to them from the greatest mercy of His being merciful. So He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." Then He mentioned man: "He created man." Then He mentioned what He did to him and what He bestowed upon him. Then He mentioned the reckoning of the sun and the moon, the prostration of things, the stars and trees; He mentioned the raising of the sky, the setting of the balance, which is justice, and the laying down of the earth for the creatures. So He addressed these two weighty ones, the jinn and humans, when they saw what came forth of power and dominion through His mercy, by which He had shown mercy to them, without any benefit or need for it. Yet they associated with Him idols and every object of worship they had taken besides Him, and they denied the mercy by which these things had come forth to them. So He asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? Their denial consisted in their making for Him, in these things which came forth from His dominion and power, a partner who possesses and has power along with Him; that is their denial. Then He mentioned the creation of man from clay, and the creation of the jinn from a smokeless fire, then asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? For He has power in every creation after creation, power after power. So the repetition in these verses is for emphasis and for intensifying the affirmation, and for establishing the proof against them by making them stand before each creation. Al-Qutabi said: God, exalted is He, enumerated in this surah His bounties and mentioned His creation as His favours; then He followed every attribute He described and every blessing He bestowed with this refrain, placing it between each two blessings, to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them, just as you say to one who keeps receiving your kindness yet denies and rejects it: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this? Were you not one who had never performed the pilgrimage (ṣarūrah) and I made the pilgrimage with you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot and I carried you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a context. He said:
"How many a blessing was yours, how many, how many!"
Another said:
"Do not kill a Muslim, if you are a Muslim woman; beware of his blood, beware, beware!"
Another said:
"Do not cut off a friend as long as your eyes weep at the words of a hateful, bitter enemy;
and do not grow weary of visiting him—visit him, visit him, visit him, visit him."
Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: repetition is for driving away heedlessness and for emphasising the proof.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 1–13 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Rahman [Azza wa Jall] is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata' and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: except for one verse in it, which is His saying, "Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him" (55:29). It has seventy-six verses. Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said: it is entirely Medinan. The first opinion is more sound, because of what 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr narrated, who said: The first person to recite the Qur'an aloud in Mecca after the Prophet (ﷺ) was Ibn Mas'ud. That was because the Companions said: "Quraysh has never heard this Qur'an recited aloud. Who will make them hear it?" Ibn Mas'ud said: "I will." They said: "We fear for you; we want a man who has a clan to protect him." He refused, then stood at the Station (al-Maqam) and said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an" (55:1–2), and he continued, raising his voice with it, while Quraysh was in its assemblies. They paid attention and said: "What is the son of Umm 'Abd saying?" They said: "He is saying what Muhammad claims was revealed to him." Then they beat him until they left marks on his face.

It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood to pray the dawn prayer at Nakhla, and recited Surat al-Rahman, and a group of jinn passed by and believed in him. In al-Tirmidhi, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from beginning to end, and they were silent. He said: "I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they were better in response than you. Every time I came to His saying, 'So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?' (55:13), they said: 'No, by nothing of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny; to You is the praise.'" He said: this is a strange (gharib) hadith. In this is evidence that it is Meccan, and Allah knows best. It was also narrated that Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Recite to me of what has been revealed to you." He recited to him Surat al-Rahman. He said: "Repeat it." He repeated it three times. He said: "By Allah, indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a sweetness, its lower part is abundant, its upper part is fruitful, and this is not the speech of a human being. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah."

It was also narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "For everything there is a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is Surat al-Rahman."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The Most Merciful (1), taught the Qur'an (2), created man (3), taught him eloquence (4).
The sun and the moon run by a reckoning (5), and the star and the tree prostrate (6), and the heaven—He raised it and set up the balance (7), that you not transgress in the balance (8), and establish the weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient (9).
And the earth—He laid it down for the creatures (10), in it is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths (11), and grain with its husk and fragrant plants (12). So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? (13)

His saying, Exalted is He: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Amir al-Sha'bi said: "al-Rahman" is the opening of three surahs which, when combined, form a name of Allah, the Exalted: (Alif-Lam-Ra) and (Ha-Mim) and (Nun), so the combined letters are "al-Rahman."

"Taught the Qur'an": that is, He taught it to His Prophet (ﷺ) until he conveyed it to all people. It was revealed when they said: "And what is the Rahman?" It was also said: it was revealed as a reply to the people of Mecca when they said: "He is only taught by a human being," and "the Rahman of Yamama," meaning Musaylima the Liar. So Allah revealed: "The Most Merciful. Taught the Qur'an."
