Al-Tha'labi reported: Ibn al-Sikkit said the Arabs call the leaves of the crop "al-'asf," "al-'asifah," and "al-jill" (with a kasra on the jim). 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah said:
"It waters channels whose 'asifah has inclined, its downward flow from the flowing water is stopped."
In al-Sihah: "al-jill" with a kasra is the stalk of the crop when it is harvested. "Al-rayhan" is provision, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Dahhak said: this is the dialect of Himyar. Also from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah: it is the sweet basil that is smelled, and Ibn Zayd said the same. Also from Ibn Abbas: it is the greenness of the crop. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands upon a stalk. Al-Farra' said: "al-'asf" is the eaten part of the crop, and "al-rayhan" is what is not eaten. Al-Kalbi said: "al-'asf" is the leaf that is not eaten, and "al-rayhan" is the edible grain. It was also said: "al-rayhan" is every fragrant-smelling herb, named so because a person finds a pleasant scent from it, i.e., smells it; so it is fa'lan, rawhan, from "al-ra'ihah" (scent). The root of the yā' in the word is a wāw, changed to yā' to distinguish it from "al-ruhani," which is everything that has a spirit (rūh). Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says "shay' ruhani" and "rayhani," meaning it has a spirit. It may also be on the pattern fay'alan, its root being "rayawhan," the wāw changed to yā' and assimilated, like hayyin and layyin; then lightening was made obligatory because of its length and the addition of the two extra letters, alif and nūn. The basic meaning of the letters rā', wāw and hā' is vibration and movement. In al-Sihah: "al-rayhan" is a well-known plant, and "al-rayhan" is provision; one says: "I went out seeking Allah's rayhan." Al-Nimr ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His rayhan, His mercy and abundant clouds."
In a hadith: "The child is from Allah's rayhan." And their saying "Subhan Allah wa rayhanahu" — they put both in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning glorification of Him and seeking provision. As for His words "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan": al-'asf is the stalk of the crop and al-rayhan its leaves, according to al-Farra'. The reading of the majority, "wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhan," with the raf' in all of them, is coordinated with "al-fakihah." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywah and al-Mughirah put all of them in the accusative, coordinated with "al-ard." It was also said: by implying a verb, i.e., "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb," and on this view it is good to pause at "dhat al-akmam." Hamzah and al-Kisa'i put "al-rayhan" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-'asf," meaning: in it is the grain possessing husk and the sweet herb. This is not excluded according to those who understand al-rayhan as provision; it would be as if he said: "and the grain possessing provision." And provision is from the fact that the husk is provision, since the husk is provision for the beasts, and the sweet herb is provision for people. There is no doubt about this for those who say it is the fragrant herb.

His saying, exalted is He: "Fa-bi-ayyi ala'i Rabbikuma tukadhdhiban" (So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?) is addressed to humans and jinn, because "al-anam" applies to both. This is the view of the majority, and it is indicated by the hadith of Jabir mentioned at the beginning of the surah, which al-Tirmidhi narrated, and in it: "The jinn were better than you in response" [[al-Tirmidhi's earlier narration differs in wording from this one; this is al-Hakim's narration]]. It was also said: when He said "He created man" and "He created the jinn," this indicated that what precedes and what follows is for both of them. Also He said: "We shall attend to you, O two burdens" [[al-thaqalan]], which is addressed to humans and jinn, and in this surah He said: "O assembly of jinn and humans." Al-Jurjani said: He addressed the jinn together with the humans even though the jinn were not previously mentioned, as in His saying: "until it was hidden behind the veil" [[see vol. 15 p. 195]]. The jinn were mentioned in what was revealed of the Qur'an earlier, and the Qur'an is like a single surah; so when it is established that they are responsible like humans, the two species are addressed with these verses. It was also said: the address is to humans, according to the Arab custom of addressing one person with the dual form, as previously mentioned regarding "alqiya fi jahannam" [[see p. 16 of this part]]. Likewise the saying:
"Halt, let us weep [[this line opens Imru' al-Qays's mu'allaqah, whose full verse is: "Qifa nabki min dhikra habibin wa manzili bi-saqt al-liwa bayna al-Dakhul fa-Hawmal"]]..."
"O my two companions, halt by Umm Jundab [[the verse opens another qasidah of Imru' al-Qays, and the full verse is: "Khalili marabi ala Umm Jundab, naqdu lubanat al-fu'ad al-mu'adhdhab"]]..."

As for what follows "He created man" and "He created the jinn," it is addressed to both humans and jinn; and the sound view is that of the majority, because of His saying: "And the earth He laid down for the creatures" (al-anam). "Al-ala'" means blessings. This is the view of all the exegetes. Its singular is ila', alan, like mi'a and 'asa, and ilyun and alyun are four dialects, related by al-Nahhas. He said: in the singular of "ana'a al-layl" there are three forms, of which the one with a fatha and an unvowelled lam is dropped; this has been discussed in al-A'raf [[see vol. 7 p. 237]] and al-Najm [[see p. 121 of this part]].

Ibn Zayd said: it means power, and the meaning of the sentence is: "So which power of your Lord will you both deny?" This was also said by al-Kalbi. Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi chose it and said: this surah, among the surahs, is the banner of the Qur'an, and the banner is the commander of the army, which the army follows. It was called a banner only because it is the surah of the attribute of sovereignty and power. He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." So He opened the surah with the name al-Rahman from among the names, so that the servants would know that all that He describes after this of His acts, of His dominion and His power, comes forth to them from the greatest mercy of His being merciful. So He said: "The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an." Then He mentioned man: "He created man." Then He mentioned what He did to him and what He bestowed upon him. Then He mentioned the reckoning of the sun and the moon, the prostration of things, the stars and trees; He mentioned the raising of the sky, the setting of the balance, which is justice, and the laying down of the earth for the creatures. So He addressed these two weighty ones, the jinn and humans, when they saw what came forth of power and dominion through His mercy, by which He had shown mercy to them, without any benefit or need for it. Yet they associated with Him idols and every object of worship they had taken besides Him, and they denied the mercy by which these things had come forth to them. So He asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? Their denial consisted in their making for Him, in these things which came forth from His dominion and power, a partner who possesses and has power along with Him; that is their denial. Then He mentioned the creation of man from clay, and the creation of the jinn from a smokeless fire, then asked them: "So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?" That is, which power of your Lord will you both deny? For He has power in every creation after creation, power after power. So the repetition in these verses is for emphasis and for intensifying the affirmation, and for establishing the proof against them by making them stand before each creation. Al-Qutabi said: God, exalted is He, enumerated in this surah His bounties and mentioned His creation as His favours; then He followed every attribute He described and every blessing He bestowed with this refrain, placing it between each two blessings, to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them, just as you say to one who keeps receiving your kindness yet denies and rejects it: "Were you not poor and I made you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure and I made you honoured? Will you deny this? Were you not one who had never performed the pilgrimage (ṣarūrah) and I made the pilgrimage with you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot and I carried you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a context. He said:
"How many a blessing was yours, how many, how many!"
Another said:
"Do not kill a Muslim, if you are a Muslim woman; beware of his blood, beware, beware!"
Another said:
"Do not cut off a friend as long as your eyes weep at the words of a hateful, bitter enemy;
and do not grow weary of visiting him—visit him, visit him, visit him, visit him."
Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: repetition is for driving away heedlessness and for emphasising the proof.

**Allah's words: ﴿He created man﴾.** When Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the creation of the great world, the heavens and the earth, and the signs they contain of His oneness and power, He then mentioned the creation of the small world, so He said: ﴿He created man﴾. By agreement of the people of ta'wil (interpretation), this means Adam.

**﴿from clay like the potter's clay﴾.** *Salsal* (dry clay) is dry earth that makes a ringing sound (*salsalah*). He likened it to fired pottery (*fakhkhar*). It has also been said that it is clay mixed with sand. It has also been said that it is foul-smelling clay, from *salla al-lahm* and *asalla*, meaning it stank. This has already been discussed in (*al-Hijr*) [[See vol. 10, p. 21.]]. Here He said ﴿from clay like the potter's clay﴾, and there He said ﴿from dry clay, from black mud, moulded﴾. He also said ﴿Indeed, We created them from sticky clay﴾ [[See vol. 15, pp. 63 and 68.]], and He said ﴿Like the example of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 102.]]. All of these have the same meaning. That is, He took dust from the earth and kneaded it until it became clay; then it changed until it became like moulded black mud; then it changed until it became dry clay like pottery.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 19–23:

The Most High said: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other. Between them is a barrier they do not transgress.﴾ *Maraja* means he left them free, released them, and neglected them. It is said: the ruler *maraja* the people when he neglected them. The root of *al-marj* is neglect, as an animal is let loose to graze (*tumraju*). It is also said that *maraja* means he mixed. Al-Akhfash said: some people say *amraja al-bahrayn*, like *maraja*, with *fa'ala* and *af'ala* having the same meaning.

"Al-bahrayn" (the two seas): Ibn 'Abbas said: the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

"Yaltaqiyan" (they meet): every year. It is also said: their two extremities meet. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the sea of Persia and the sea of Rome. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the salt sea and the sweet rivers. It is also said: the sea of the east and the sea of the west, whose extremities meet. It is also said: the sea of pearls and the sea of coral.

"Baynahuma barzakh" (between them is a barrier), that is, a partition. According to the first view, it is what lies between the sky and the earth, as said by al-Dahhak. According to the second view, it is the land between them, which is the Hijaz, as said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. According to the other views, it is the divine power, as was discussed earlier in (*al-Furqan*) [[See vol. 13, p. 58.]]. There is a report from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that Allah the Most High spoke to the western direction and said: "I will place in you servants of Mine who glorify Me, magnify Me, declare My oneness, and praise Me. How will you be towards them?" It replied: "I will drown them, O Lord." He said: "I will carry them on My hand and place Your might in your regions." Then He spoke to the eastern direction and said: "I will place in you servants who glorify Me, magnify Me, declare My oneness, and praise Me. How will you be towards them?" It said: "I will glorify You with them when they glorify You, I will magnify You with them when they magnify You, I will declare Your oneness with them when they declare Your oneness, and I will praise You with them when they praise You." So Allah rewarded it with the ornament, placed a barrier between them, one of them turned into salty bitter water, and the other remained in its state, sweet and fresh. This report was mentioned by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah, who said: Salih ibn Muhammad related to us, al-Qasim al-'Umari related to us, from Sahl, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah.

"La yabghiyan" (they do not transgress): Qatadah said: they do not transgress against the people so as to drown them; He placed between them and the people dry land [[In manuscripts b, h, z, s, l, h: "al-yabs" (dryness).]]. It is also reported from him and from Mujahid: neither of them transgresses against the other so as to overpower it. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of "la yabghiyan" is that they do not seek to meet, and the sense of the speech is: "He released the two seas, meeting each other," were it not for the barrier between them, they would not seek to meet. It is also said: the barrier is what lies between this world and the Hereafter, that is, between them there is a term that Allah has decreed, which is the duration of this world, so they do not transgress. When Allah permits the end of this world, the two seas become one thing. This is like His saying: ﴿And when the seas are burst forth﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 242.]]. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: the two seas are the path of good and evil, and the barrier between them is success (*tawfiq*) and divine protection (*'isma*).

The Most High said: ﴿From both of them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [that is, from the water there emerges for you the pearl and the coral], just as from the earth emerge the grain, the husk, and the fragrant plants. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read *yukhraju* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ra'*, as a passive verb. The rest read *yakhruju* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *ra'*, meaning that the pearl is the subject. He said "minhuma" (from both of them), though the pearl only emerges from the salt water, not the sweet, because the Arabs combine the two kinds and then speak about one of them, as in His saying: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾, although the messengers were from humankind only, not from the jinn. This was said by al-Kalbi and others. Al-Zajjaj said: Allah mentioned both, so when something comes out of one of them, it has come out of both. This is like His saying: ﴿Do you not see how Allah created seven heavens in layers, and placed the moon therein as a light?﴾, while the moon is in the lowest heaven, but the mention of the seven was summarized, so what is in one of them is as though it were in them all. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: this is from the category of omitting the qualifier, that is, from one of the two, like His saying: ﴿on a great man of the two towns﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 82.]], that is, from one of the two towns.

Al-Akhfash Sa'id said: some people claim that pearls emerge from the sweet water. It is also said: they are two seas, from one of which the pearl emerges and from the other the coral. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth. When rainwater falls into the shell of the sea, it solidifies into a pearl, so it emerges from both of them. This was also said by al-Tabari. al-Tha'labi said: I was told that a seed was inside a shell, and a drop fell on part of the seed but not on the rest, so where the drop struck the seed there was a pearl, and the rest remained seed. It is also said: the sweet and the salt water may meet, and the sweet acts as the fertilizing element for the salt, so it is attributed to both, just as a child is attributed to the male and the female even if the female bore it. For this reason it is said: pearls only emerge from a place where sweet and salt water meet. It is also said: coral is the large and great pearls, as said by 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and pearl is the small ones. And from both of them also, in reverse: the pearl is the large pearls and the coral is the small ones, as said by al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Malik said: coral is red beads.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 24–25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And His are the ships (al-jawar)﴾, meaning the ships.

(al-munsha'at) is the reading of the majority, (al-munsha'at) with a fatha on the shin. Qatadah said: that is, the created things for running, derived from al-inshā' (bringing into being). Mujahid said: they are the ships whose sails are raised, and he said: if their sails are not raised, they are not munsha'at. Al-Akhfash said: they are the ones that run. In a hadith: that 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, saw ships with their sails raised, and he said: "By the Lord of these jawari munsha'at, I did not kill 'Uthman, nor did I collude in his killing." Hamzah and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim with a variation from him, read (al-munshi'at) with a kasra on the shin, meaning the ones that produce the motion, the verb being attributed to them by way of metaphor and extension. It was also said: the ones that raise the sails (al-shura'), that is, the sails. Whoever reads the shin with a fatha says: the ones that are raised, the sails.

(ka-al-a'lam) means like the mountains, and al-'alam is a tall mountain. The poet said [[the speaker is Jarir; the full verse is:

hatta tanahayna bina ila al-Hakam

and after it:

khalifat al-Hajjaj ghayr al-muttaham ... fi dau' al-majd wa-bu'bu' al-karam]]:

"When they cross a mountain, a landmark appears."

So the ships in the sea are like the mountains on land. Its explanation has already passed in (al-Shura) [[see vol. 16, p. 23]]. Ya'qub read (al-jawari) with a yā' in pause, and the rest omitted it.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 55, verses 26–28**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish.﴾ The pronoun in "upon it" (عَلَيْها) refers to the earth, whose mention has already occurred at the beginning of the surah in His saying, Exalted is He: "And the earth He laid out for the creatures" (وَالْأَرْضَ وَضَعَها لِلْأَنامِ). It may also be said that "he is the most honoured of those upon it," meaning the earth, even though no prior mention of it has occurred.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When this verse was revealed, the angels said, "The people of the earth have perished." Then it was revealed: "Everything will perish except His Face" (كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ) (See vol. 13, p. 322). Thereupon the angels were certain of the perishing. Muqatil also said this. The benefit (wajh al-ni'mah) in the perishing of creation is the equalising of people in death, and with death, feet become equal. It was also said: the benefit is that death is the cause of transfer to the abode of recompense and reward.

(And there remains the Face of your Lord) That is, and Allah remains. So "the Face" is an expression for His existence and His essence, glory be to Him. The poet said:

"He decreed over His creation the deaths, so everything other than Him is perishing."

This is what the verifying scholars of our school have chosen: Ibn Fawrak, Abu al-Ma'ali, and others. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "The Face" is an expression for Him, as He said: "And there remains the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honour" (وَيَبْقى وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ ذُو الْجَلالِ وَالْإِكْرامِ). Abu al-Ma'ali said: As for "the Face," what is meant by it, according to the majority of our imams, is the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, and this is what our shaykh chose. Among the evidence for this is His saying, "And there remains the Face of your Lord," and the one described with remaining, when creation is exposed to perishing, is the existence of the Creator, exalted is He. The discussion of this has already passed in (al-Baqarah) (See vol. 2, p. 83) at His saying, Exalted is He: "Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah" (فَأَيْنَما تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ), and we have mentioned it fully in the book al-Asna (the Most Beautiful). Al-Qushayri said: A people said it is an attribute additional to the essence, which is not described as to its modality (la tukayyaf), by which turning toward whoever the Lord wishes to specially honour is achieved. The correct view is that it is said: "His Face" is His existence and His essence. It is said: "This is the face of the matter," "the face of the correct course," and "the essence of the correct course." It was also said: that is, the manifest is preserved through His proofs, as a person is manifest through his face. And it was said: the direction by which one draws near to Allah remains.

(Full of Majesty) Al-Jalal is the greatness of Allah, His magnificence, and His being deserving of attributes of praise. It is said: "Jalla al-shay'" meaning it became great, and "ajlaltuhu" meaning I glorified him. Al-Jalal is a noun from jalla.

(and Honour) That is, He is worthy of being honoured above what is not fitting for Him of polytheism, as you say: "I honour you from this." From it comes the honouring of the prophets and the friends of Allah. We have addressed these two names linguistically and in meaning fully in the book al-Asna. It is narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Persist in calling upon Him, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour" (أَلِظُّوا بيا ذَا الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ). **Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 55, verses 26–28**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish.﴾ The pronoun in "upon it" (عَلَيْها) refers to the earth, whose mention has already occurred at the beginning of the surah in His saying, Exalted is He: "And the earth He laid out for the creatures" (وَالْأَرْضَ وَضَعَها لِلْأَنامِ). It may also be said that "he is the most honoured of those upon it," meaning the earth, even though no prior mention of it has occurred.

Ibn 'Abbas said: When this verse was revealed, the angels said, "The people of the earth have perished." Then it was revealed: "Everything will perish except His Face" (كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ) (See vol. 13, p. 322). Thereupon the angels were certain of the perishing. Muqatil also said this. The benefit (wajh al-ni'mah) in the perishing of creation is the equalising of people in death, and with death, feet become equal. It was also said: the benefit is that death is the cause of transfer to the abode of recompense and reward.

(And there remains the Face of your Lord) That is, and Allah remains. So "the Face" is an expression for His existence and His essence, glory be to Him. The poet said:

"He decreed over His creation the deaths, so everything other than Him is perishing."

This is what the verifying scholars of our school have chosen: Ibn Fawrak, Abu al-Ma'ali, and others. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "The Face" is an expression for Him, as He said: "And there remains the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honour" (وَيَبْقى وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ ذُو الْجَلالِ وَالْإِكْرامِ). Abu al-Ma'ali said: As for "the Face," what is meant by it, according to the majority of our imams, is the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, and this is what our shaykh chose. Among the evidence for this is His saying, "And there remains the Face of your Lord," and the one described with remaining, when creation is exposed to perishing, is the existence of the Creator, exalted is He. The discussion of this has already passed in (al-Baqarah) (See vol. 2, p. 83) at His saying, Exalted is He: "Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah" (فَأَيْنَما تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ), and we have mentioned it fully in the book al-Asna (the Most Beautiful). Al-Qushayri said: A people said it is an attribute additional to the essence, which is not described as to its modality (la tukayyaf), by which turning toward whoever the Lord wishes to specially honour is achieved. The correct view is that it is said: "His Face" is His existence and His essence. It is said: "This is the face of the matter," "the face of the correct course," and "the essence of the correct course." It was also said: that is, the manifest is preserved through His proofs, as a person is manifest through his face. And it was said: the direction by which one draws near to Allah remains.

(Full of Majesty) Al-Jalal is the greatness of Allah, His magnificence, and His being deserving of attributes of praise. It is said: "Jalla al-shay'" meaning it became great, and "ajlaltuhu" meaning I glorified him. Al-Jalal is a noun from jalla.

(and Honour) That is, He is worthy of being honoured above what is not fitting for Him of polytheism, as you say: "I honour you from this." From it comes the honouring of the prophets and the friends of Allah. We have addressed these two names linguistically and in meaning fully in the book al-Asna. It is narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Persist in calling upon Him, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour" (أَلِظُّوا بيا ذَا الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ). It is also narrated that this is from the words of Ibn Mas'ud, and its meaning is: keep to this in supplication. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-ilzaz is keeping to a thing and persevering in it. It is also said: al-ilzaz is insistence. From Sa'id al-Maqbari: a man insisted and kept saying, "O Allah, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour! O Allah, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour!" So he was called: "Indeed I have heard you; what is your need?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 29–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾. It has been said: the meaning is that whoever is in the heavens asks Him for mercy (rahmah), and whoever is on the earth asks Him for provision (rizq). Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: the people of the heavens ask Him for forgiveness but do not ask Him for provision, while the people of the earth ask Him for both. Ibn Juraij said: the angels ask Him for provision for the people of the earth, so both requests, from the people of the heavens and the people of the earth, were for the people of the earth.

And in a hadith: "Among the angels is an angel who has four faces: a face like the face of a human, which asks Allah for provision for the children of Adam; a face like the face of a lion, which asks Allah for provision for the predatory beasts; a face like the face of a bull, which asks Allah for provision for the livestock; and a face like the face of an eagle, which asks Allah for provision for the birds." Ibn 'Ata' said: they asked Him for the strength to worship.

﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾. This is a new (independent) statement. The phrase "every day" (kulla yawm) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, either governed by the word "in a matter" (fi sha'n), or as an adverb of time for the asking, and then a new statement begins: "He is in a matter."

Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said regarding "Every day He is in a matter": "Among His matters is that He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises some people and lowers others." And from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "Every day He is in a matter," he said: "He forgives a sin, removes a distress, and answers a supplicant." It has been said: among His matters is that He gives life and causes death, honours and humbles, provides and withholds. It has also been said: He meant His matter in the two days of this world and the Hereafter. Ibn Bahr said: the whole of time is two days, one of which is the span of the days of this world, and the other is the Day of Resurrection. So His matter, glorified and exalted is He, in the days of this world is trial and testing through command and prohibition, giving life and causing death, giving and withholding; and His matter on the Day of Resurrection is recompense and reckoning, reward and punishment. It has been said: what is meant by this is the report of His matter on every day of the days of this world, and this is the apparent meaning.

The word sha'n (matter) in the language means a great affair, and its plural is shu'un, and the meaning of sha'n here is the plural, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 330]. Al-Kalbi said: His matter is driving decrees toward their appointed times. 'Amr ibn Maymun said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾: among His matters is that He causes the living to die, settles what He wills in the wombs, honours the humble, and humbles the honoured.

One of the rulers asked his vizier about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾, and he did not know its meaning, and asked for a delay until the next day. So he went back to his home dejected, and his black slave said to him: "What is your matter?" So he informed him. He said to him: "Return to the ruler, for I will explain it to him." So he summoned him, and he said: "O ruler! His matter is that He causes the night to enter the day, and causes the day to enter the night, brings the living out of the dead, brings the dead out of the living, cures the sick, makes the healthy ill, tests the one who is well, grants well-being to the one who is tested, honours the humble, humbles the honoured, makes the wealthy poor, and makes the poor wealthy." So the ruler said to him: "You have relieved me, may Allah relieve you," then he ordered the vizier's garments to be stripped off and given to the slave. He said: "O my master! This is of the matter of Allah, exalted is He."

And from 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir: that he summoned al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl and said to him: "Three verses have become difficult for me, and I have called you to clarify them for me: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he became of the regretful﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 143], and it is established that regret is repentance. And His saying: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾, and it is established that the Pen has dried with what will occur until the Day of Resurrection. And His saying: ﴿And that man has nothing except what he strives for﴾ [see vol. 17, p. ], so what of the multiplied reward?" Al-Husayn said: "It is possible that regret was not repentance for that nation, and that it is repentance for this nation, because Allah, exalted is He, singled out this nation with distinctions in which other nations did not share." It has also been said: the regret of Qabil was not over killing Habil, but over carrying him (the burden of his body). As for His saying: ﴿Every day He is in a matter﴾, these are matters that He manifests, not matters that He initiates. As for His saying: ﴿And that man has nothing except what he strives for﴾, its meaning is: he has nothing except what he strives for as justice, and it is open to Me to recompense him with one thousandfold as grace. Then 'Abd Allah stood up, kissed his head, and gave him a grant of wealth.

**Qur'anic verse 31–36 (Surah ar-Rahman, 55)**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿We will surely attend to you, O you two weighty ones﴾. It is said: *faraghtu min ash-shughl* (I became free of the task) *afruʿu furuʿan wa faraghan*, and *tafarraghtu li-kadhā* (I devoted myself to such-and-such), and *istafraghtu majhūdī fī kadhā* (I exerted my full effort in such-and-such), meaning I expended it. God, Exalted is He, has no task from which He becomes free. Rather the meaning is: "We will intend to requite you or to call you to account." This is a warning and a threat to them, just as a speaker says to someone he wishes to threaten: "Then I will attend to you," meaning "I will target you." *Faragha* here means *qasada* (he intended). Ibn al-Anbari cited in this regard a verse of Jarir:

*Now that I have turned my attention to Numayr,*
*this is the time when I was a torment to her.*

He means: "now that I have intended." Jarir also said, and al-Nahhas cited it:

*I turned my attention to the shackled slave in the anklets.*

It is related in a hadith that when the Prophet (ﷺ) pledged allegiance with the Ansar on the night of al-Aqabah, Satan shouted: "O people of al-Jabajib!" (the Jabajib are the lodgings of Mina) "This Mudhammam is pledging allegiance to the Banu Qaylah to fight against you!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is Izb al-Aqabah (the Azb was vocalised by al-Halabi in his Sira with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the zay; here it is the name of a devil). By God, O enemy of God, I will surely attend to you," meaning: "I will intend to nullify your affair." This is the view preferred by al-Qutaybi, al-Kisa'i and others.

It was also said: God promised reward for piety and threatened punishment for wickedness, then said, "We will surely attend to you" regarding what We have promised you, and We will bring each party to what We promised it. That is, I swear to it and will attend to it. This was said by al-Hasan, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) and Ubayy read *sa-nafrughu ilaykum*. Al-Aʿmash and Ibrahim read *sa-yuflaghu lakum*, with a damma on the yaʾ and a fatha on the raʾ, in the passive voice. Ibn Shihab and al-Aʿraj read *sa-nafraghu lakum* with a fatha on the nun and the raʾ. Al-Kisa'i said: this is the dialect of Tamim, who say *faragha yafraghu*, and he also transmitted *faragha yafraghu*. Hubayrah transmitted both from Hafs from ʿAsim. Al-Juʿfi transmitted from Abu ʿAmr *sa-yafraghu* with a fatha on the yaʾ and the raʾ, and it was also transmitted from Ibn Hurmuz. It is transmitted from ʿIsa al-Thaqafi: *sa-nifraghu lakum* with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the raʾ. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *sa-yafrughu lakum* with a yaʾ. The rest read with a nun, and this is the dialect of Tihama.

*Al-thaqalan* are the jinn and mankind. They were so named because of the greatness of their status compared with other creatures on earth, by reason of being charged with obligations. It was also said that they were named this because they are a burden upon the earth, both living and dead. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the earth brought forth its burdens﴾ (see vol. 20, p. 147). From this comes the saying: "Give him his *thiql*," meaning his weight. Some scholars of meanings said: everything that has measure and weight and is coveted is a *thiql*. From this it is said that ostrich eggs are a *thiql*, because the one who finds and hunts them rejoices in them when he obtains them. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: they were named the two burdens because they are weighed down with sins. He said, "We will attend to you" in the plural, then said, "O you two weighty ones," because they are two groups, and each group is a plurality. Likewise the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able﴾, and He did not say "if you two are able," because they are two groups in the state of plurality, as in His words: ﴿Then behold, they are two parties disputing﴾ (see vol. 13, p. 214), and ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ (see vol. 12, p. 25 and p. 238, and vol. 16, p. 97). Had He said "We will attend to you two" and "if you two are able," it would have been permissible (outside the Qur'an).

The people of Syria read *ayyuhu al-thaqalan* with a damma on the ha'. The rest read it with a fatha. This has already been discussed (see vol. 12, p. 25 and p. 238, and vol. 16, p. 97).

*Issue*: This surah, along with *al-Ahqaf* and *Qul Uhiya*, is evidence that the jinn are addressed, bound by obligations, commanded, forbidden, rewarded and punished just like mankind. Their believers are like the believers among mankind, and their disbelievers like the disbelievers among mankind. There is no difference between us and them in any of this.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾, the verse. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Juwaybir informed us from al-Dahhak, who said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, God commands the lowest heaven, and it splits open with its inhabitants. The angels will be on its edges until the Lord commands them. They will descend to the earth and surround the earth and those upon it. Then God commands the heaven next to it, and in the same way they descend and form a row behind that row (in another manuscript: "in the midst of that row"). Then the third heaven, then the fourth, then the fifth, then the sixth, then the seventh. The Supreme King descends in His splendour and sovereignty, and on His left side is Hell. They hear its roaring and its sighing, and they cannot reach any region of it without finding rows of angels. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass; you will not pass except with authority﴾. *Sultan* means excuse.

Al-Dahhak also said: While people are in their markets, the sky opens and the angels descend, and the jinn and mankind flee, and the angels encircle them. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿You will not pass except with authority﴾. Al-Nahhas mentioned this. I (al-Qurtubi) say: according to this, it occurs in this world; and according to what Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned, it occurs in the Hereafter.

It is also related from al-Dahhak: If you are able to flee from death, then flee. Ibn ʿAbbas said: If you are able to know what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, then know it; but you will not know it except with *sultan*, that is, with clear proof from God, Exalted is He. It is also related from him that the meaning of ﴿You will not pass except with authority﴾ is: "You will not leave My authority and My power over you." Qatadah said: "You will not pass except with a king, and you have no king." It was also said: "You will not pass except toward a sultan," the *ba'* being in the sense of *ila* (toward), as in His words: ﴿and He has been good to me﴾ (see vol. 9, p. 267), meaning "to me." The poet (Kuthayyir ʿAzzah) said:

*Treat us badly or treat us well; she is not one who tires of us, nor is she one who is hated when she grows weary.*

His words "fa-nfudhu" (then pass) are a command of incapacitation.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿There will be sent upon you both a flame of fire and molten brass﴾. That is: if you went out, a flame of fire would be sent upon you, and the punishment that prevents passage would seize you. It was also said: this is not connected to passing through; rather, He informs that He punishes the disobedient with fire. It was also said: meaning, "By which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny? A flame of fire and brass will be sent upon you two as punishment for that denial." Al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin say: "*Salit* is sesame oil in Syria, and there is no smoke in it."

Muqatil said: They are five rivers of molten copper flowing from beneath the Throne over the heads of the people of the Fire: three rivers in the measure of the night and two in the measure of the day. Ibn Mas'ud said: *nuhas* is *muhl* (dregs of molten metal). Al-Dahhak said: it is the sediment of boiling oil. Al-Kisa'i said: it is the fire that has a strong wind.

﴿So you two will not be able to help each other﴾, that is: one of you will not help the other, meaning the jinn and mankind.

**Qur'anic verse 31–36 (Surah ar-Rahman, 55)**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿We will surely attend to you, O you two weighty ones﴾. God, Exalted is He, has no task from which He becomes free. Rather the meaning is: "We will intend to requite you or to call you to account." This is a warning and a threat to them, just as a speaker says to someone he wishes to threaten: "Then I will attend to you," meaning "I will target you." *Faragha* here means *qasada* (he intended). Ibn al-Anbari cited in this regard a verse of Jarir:

*Now that I have turned my attention to Numayr,*
*this is the time when I was a torment to her.*

He means: "now that I have intended." Jarir also said, and al-Nahhas cited it:

*I turned my attention to the shackled slave in the anklets.*

It is related in a hadith that when the Prophet (ﷺ) pledged allegiance with the Ansar on the night of al-Aqabah, Satan shouted: "O people of al-Jabajib!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is Izb al-Aqabah (the Azb was vocalised by al-Halabi in his Sira with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the zay; here it is the name of a devil). It was also said: God promised reward for piety and threatened punishment for wickedness, then said, "We will surely attend to you" regarding what We have promised you, and We will bring each party to what We promised it. That is, I swear to it and will attend to it. This was said by al-Hasan, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd.

The rest read with a nun, and this is the dialect of Tihama.

From this it is said that ostrich eggs are a *thiql*, because the one who finds and hunts them rejoices in them when he obtains them. He said, "We will attend to you" in the plural, then said, "O you two weighty ones," because they are two groups, and each group is a plurality. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 37–40:

Allah's words: ﴿And when the sky splits open﴾, that is, it is cleft on the Day of Resurrection. (﴿And it becomes rose-red like tanned leather﴾). *Al-dihan* means *al-duhn* (oil), according to Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others. The meaning is that it becomes like the clarity of oil, and on this view *al-dihan* is the plural of *duhn*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: the meaning is that it becomes red. It was also said: the meaning is that it takes on the redness of the rose and the flowing of oil, that is, it melts with the splitting until it becomes red from the heat of the fire of Hell, and becomes like oil in its thinness and melting. It was also said: *al-dihan* is pure red leather, as mentioned by Abu Ubayd and al-Farra', that is, the sky becomes red like hide because of the intense heat of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is that it becomes like a rose-coloured horse. A chestnut horse is called *ward* (rose-coloured) if it shows various colours. Ibn Abbas said: a rose-coloured horse in spring is a yellowish chestnut, at the start of winter it is a reddish chestnut, and when winter intensifies it becomes a dusty chestnut. Al-Farra' said: he meant the rose-coloured horse (*al-faras al-wardiyyah*), which in spring is rose-coloured tending to yellow, and when the cold intensifies it becomes a red rose-colour, and after that it becomes rose-coloured tending to dust-grey. So the changing colour of the sky is compared to the changing colour of rose-coloured horses. Al-Hasan said: (﴿like tanned leather﴾) means like the pouring of oil, for when you pour it you see colours in it. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the meaning is that it becomes like the dregs of olive oil. It was also said: the meaning is that it passes and comes (*tamurru wa tajii'*). Al-Zajjaj said: the root *w-r-d* is for coming and arriving. This is close to what we mentioned earlier, that the rose-coloured horse changes its colours. Qatadah said: it is green today, and it will have a red colour; this was related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Mawardi said: the early scholars held that the original colour of the sky is red, and that because of the many barriers and the great distance it appears in this blue colour. They compared this to the veins of the body, which are red like the redness of blood but appear blue through the covering. If this is correct, then on the Day of Resurrection, because the sky is near the eyes and the barriers are removed, it will appear red, since red is its original colour. And Allah knows best.

This is like His saying: ﴿And the guilty will not be asked about their sins﴾ (See vol. 13, p. 316), and that the Resurrection has stations because that day is long, so they are questioned in some stations and not questioned in others. This is the view of Ikrimah. It was also said: the meaning is that they are not questioned once they have settled into the Fire. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they are not asked about their sins, because Allah has preserved them and the angels have recorded them against them. This was related by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Also from al-Hasan and Mujahid: the meaning is that the angels do not ask about them, because they recognise them by their marks, and the evidence for this is what follows it. Mujahid also said this from Ibn Abbas. And from him too, regarding Allah's words ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ (See vol. 10, p. 59), and His words ﴿So on that day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾, he said: He does not question them in order to learn that from them, for He knows it better than they do, but He questions them as a rebuke, asking: "Why did you do it?" Abu al-Aliyah said: no one other than the guilty is questioned about the sin of the guilty. Qatadah said: there was questioning before, then the mouths of the people were sealed and the limbs spoke, testifying against them.

In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ), in which he said: "He meets the servant and says, 'O so-and-so' [*ayyu fulun*: meaning 'O such-and-such', not a diminutive of him; it is a form used for calling, and it is only said with the lam silent. Some said it is a diminutive of *fulan*], 'Did I not honour you, make you a leader, marry you, subject to you horses and camels, and leave you to preside and to lead in turn?' He says, 'Yes.' He says, 'Did you think that you would meet Me?' He says, 'No.' He says, 'Then I will forget you as you forgot Me.' Then he meets the second and says to him the same thing exactly. Then he meets the third and says the same to him. He says, 'O Lord, I believed in You, in Your Book and in Your Messenger, and I prayed, fasted and gave charity,' and he praises himself with the best he can. Then it is said to him, 'Now We shall send Our witness against you.' He reflects within himself: who is this who will testify against me? His mouth is sealed, and it is said to his thigh, his flesh and his bones: 'Speak!' And his thigh, his flesh and his bones speak of his deeds. This is so that he has no excuse from himself, and that is the hypocrite, and the one with whom Allah is angry." This hadith has already been mentioned in (Ha Mim, the surah of prostration) and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 37–40:

Allah's words: ﴿And when the sky splits open﴾, that is, it is cleft on the Day of Resurrection. (﴿And it becomes rose-red like tanned leather﴾). *Al-dihan* means *al-duhn* (oil), according to Mujahid, al-Dahhak and others. The meaning is that it becomes like the clarity of oil, and on this view *al-dihan* is the plural of *duhn*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: the meaning is that it becomes red. It was also said: the meaning is that it takes on the redness of the rose and the flowing of oil, that is, it melts with the splitting until it becomes red from the heat of the fire of Hell, and becomes like oil in its thinness and melting. It was also said: *al-dihan* is pure red leather, as mentioned by Abu Ubayd and al-Farra', that is, the sky becomes red like hide because of the intense heat of the Fire. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is that it becomes like a rose-coloured horse. A chestnut horse is called *ward* (rose-coloured) if it shows various colours. Ibn Abbas said: a rose-coloured horse in spring is a yellowish chestnut, at the start of winter it is a reddish chestnut, and when winter intensifies it becomes a dusty chestnut. Al-Farra' said: he meant the rose-coloured horse (*al-faras al-wardiyyah*), which in spring is rose-coloured tending to yellow, and when the cold intensifies it becomes a red rose-colour, and after that it becomes rose-coloured tending to dust-grey. So the changing colour of the sky is compared to the changing colour of rose-coloured horses. Al-Hasan said: (﴿like tanned leather﴾) means like the pouring of oil, for when you pour it you see colours in it. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the meaning is that it becomes like the dregs of olive oil. It was also said: the meaning is that it passes and comes (*tamurru wa tajii'*). Al-Zajjaj said: the root *w-r-d* is for coming and arriving. This is close to what we mentioned earlier, that the rose-coloured horse changes its colours. Qatadah said: it is green today, and it will have a red colour; this was related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Mawardi said: the early scholars held that the original colour of the sky is red, and that because of the many barriers and the great distance it appears in this blue colour. They compared this to the veins of the body, which are red like the redness of blood but appear blue through the covering. If this is correct, then on the Day of Resurrection, because the sky is near the eyes and the barriers are removed, it will appear red, since red is its original colour. And Allah knows best.

This is like His saying: ﴿And the guilty will not be asked about their sins﴾ (See vol. 13, p. 316), and that the Resurrection has stations because that day is long, so they are questioned in some stations and not questioned in others. This is the view of Ikrimah. It was also said: the meaning is that they are not questioned once they have settled into the Fire. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they are not asked about their sins, because Allah has preserved them and the angels have recorded them against them. This was related by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Abu al-Aliyah said: no one other than the guilty is questioned about the sin of the guilty. Qatadah said: there was questioning before, then the mouths of the people were sealed and the limbs spoke, testifying against them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 55, verses 46–47:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾. In this verse there are two issues (masalatan).

The first: When He mentioned the states of the people of the Fire, He mentioned what He has prepared for the righteous (al-abrar). The meaning is: one who fears his standing before his Lord for the reckoning, and so abandons disobedience. Here "maqam" is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning "standing" (al-qiyam). It was also said: he fears his Lord's standing over him, that is, His oversight and His observing of him. Its explanation is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who have no partners]?﴾ [See vol. 9, p. 322.] Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: it is the man who intends to commit an act of disobedience, then remembers God and refrains from it out of fear of Him.

The second: This verse is evidence that whoever says to his wife, "If I am not among the people of Paradise, then you are divorced," does not break his oath if he had intended an act of disobedience and abandoned it out of fear of God and shame before Him. Sufyan al-Thawri said this and issued a legal ruling (afta) accordingly. Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Tirmidhi said: one garden is for his fear of his Lord, and one garden is for his abandoning of desire.

Ibn 'Abbas said: [it is] one who fears the standing of his Lord after performing the obligatory duties (al-fara'id). It was also said: "maqam" means "place," that is, he fears his place before his Lord for the reckoning, as previously mentioned. It is permissible that "maqam" refers to the servant and then is attributed to God, as in the case of "ajal" (term) in His saying: ﴿So when their term comes﴾ [See vol. 7, p. 202.] and His saying in another place: ﴿Indeed, the term of God, when it comes, is not delayed﴾ [See vol. 18, p. (299).]

"Two gardens" means: for the one who fears there are two gardens, each distinct; so every fearer has two gardens. It was also said: two gardens for all the fearers collectively, but the first view is more apparent.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The two gardens are two gardens in the breadth of Paradise; each garden is a journey of one hundred years, and in the middle of each garden is a dwelling of light, and there is nothing in it but that it quivers with melody and greenery; its dwelling is firm and its trees are firm." Al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi also mentioned it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra.

It was also said: the two gardens are the garden that was created for him and a garden that he inherited. It was said: one of the two gardens is his dwelling and the other is the dwelling of his wives, as the leaders of this world do. It was said: one of the two gardens is his residence and the other is his orchard. It was said: one of the two gardens is the lower parts of the palaces and the other is their upper parts.

Muqatil said: they are the Garden of Eden (jannat 'adn) and the Garden of Delight (jannat al-na'im).

Al-Farra' said: it is really one garden, but the dual was used for the sake of the verse-endings (ru'us al-ayy). Al-Qutaybi rejected this and said: it is not permissible to say "the guardians of the Fire are twenty," for He only said "nineteen" out of regard for the verse-endings. He also said: [God says] "dhawata afnan" [Surah 55:48, "having branches"]. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: al-Farra' said that it may be one garden and be made dual in poetry. This statement is among the greatest errors regarding the Book of God, the Mighty and Majestic: God says "two gardens" and describes them by His saying "in them," so he leaves the apparent meaning and says: it is permissible that it be one garden, and argues from poetry!

It was also said: they were two only so that his joy would be multiplied through moving from one place to another.

It was said: it was revealed specifically concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, when one day he mentioned Paradise, when it was brought near, and the Fire, when it was made manifest. This was said by 'Ata' and Ibn Shawdhab. Al-Dahhak said: rather, one day he drank milk while thirsty and liked it, so he asked about it and was informed that it had been obtained unlawfully, so he vomited it up, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was looking at him. He said: "May God have mercy on you! Indeed a verse was revealed concerning you," and he recited to him this verse.

**Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 55, verses 52–55**

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿In both of them are two kinds of every fruit﴾, meaning two varieties, and both are sweet and pleasant to eat. Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is no tree in this world, sweet or bitter, that is not in Paradise, even the colocynth (al-handhal), except that it is sweet." It is also said: "There are two kinds, fresh and dry, and neither is inferior to the other in excellence and goodness." It is also said: He intended to honour these two gardens above the two gardens below them. Here He mentioned two flowing springs, while there He mentioned two springs that spurt with water, and spurting is less than flowing. So it is as if He said: in those two gardens there is one kind of every fruit, and in this garden there are two kinds of every fruit.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿reclining on couches﴾. This is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). Al-furush is the plural of firash. Abu Haywa read (furshin) with a sukun on the rā'.

(Batā'inuhā) is the plural of bitana (lining), which is the layer beneath the outer covering (ẓihāra). Al-istabraq is thick, coarse brocade. That is, if the lining that faces the ground is like this, then what do you think of the outer covering? This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra. It was said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The linings are of istabraq, so what are the outer surfaces?" He said: "This is among what Allah has spoken of: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾." Ibn 'Abbas said: "He only described for you their linings so that your hearts might be guided to it, but as for the outer surfaces, none knows them except Allah." It is reported in a khabar from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Their outer surfaces are a shining light." From al-Hasan: their linings are of istabraq and their outer surfaces are of solid light. Also from al-Hasan: the linings are the outer surfaces. This is the view of al-Farra', and it is also reported from Qatada. The Arabs call the back of a thing its belly (baṭn), so they say: "This is the back of the sky" and "This is the belly of the sky," referring to its outer side which we see. Ibn Qutayba and others rejected this, saying: this is only used for two equal sides, when each of the two faces a people, like a wall between you and a people, and this is the case with the sky.

(Wa-janā al-jannatayni dān): al-janā is what is picked from a tree. It is said: "He brought us a good harvest (janāh ṭayyiba)" for whatever is gathered. A fruit that has been picked is called janiyy, on the pattern fa'il, when it has been plucked. And [the poet] said [[This is the poet 'Amr ibn 'Adi al-Lakhmi, son of the sister of Judhayma al-Abrash. It is a proverb used for a man who gives his companion the best of what he has.]]:

"This is my harvest, and its best is in it, since every picker brings his hand to his mouth."

It was also read as (jinā) with a kasra on the jīm.

(Dān): near. Ibn 'Abbas said: The tree will draw near until the friend of Allah can pick from it, whether standing, sitting, or lying down. Neither distance nor thorns will keep his hand from it.

**Al-Qurtubi's Commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 55, verses 52–55**

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿In both of them are two kinds of every fruit﴾, meaning two varieties, and both are sweet and pleasant to eat. Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is no tree in this world, sweet or bitter, that is not in Paradise, even the colocynth (al-handhal), except that it is sweet." It is also said: "There are two kinds, fresh and dry, and neither is inferior to the other in excellence and goodness." It is also said: He intended to honour these two gardens above the two gardens below them. Here He mentioned two flowing springs, while there He mentioned two springs that spurt with water, and spurting is less than flowing. So it is as if He said: in those two gardens there is one kind of every fruit, and in this garden there are two kinds of every fruit.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿reclining on couches﴾. This is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). Al-furush is the plural of firash. Abu Haywa read (furshin) with a sukun on the rā'.

(Batā'inuhā) is the plural of bitana (lining), which is the layer beneath the outer covering (ẓihāra). Al-istabraq is thick, coarse brocade. That is, if the lining that faces the ground is like this, then what do you think of the outer covering? This was said by Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayra. It was said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The linings are of istabraq, so what are the outer surfaces?" **First issue:** Concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾. It was said: "Therein" refers to the two gardens mentioned. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "therein" (fihinna) and not "in them" (fihima), because He meant the two gardens and what was prepared for their owner of bliss. It was also said: "therein" refers to the couches whose linings are of brocade (istabraq), that is, in these couches are women restraining their gaze, who have restrained their eyes to their husbands so that they see no one else. This was discussed in (al-Saffat) [see vol. 15, p. 80], and "gaze" (tarf) is given in the singular despite its being attached to a plural because it carries the sense of a verbal noun, from "his eye blinked" (taraftat ʿaynuhu taṭrifu ṭarfan). Then the eye was called by this name, so it serves for both the singular and the plural, as in the expression "a just people" (qawm ʿadl) and "fasting people" (qawm ṣawm).

**Second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Untouched before them by any human or jinn﴾ (lam yaṭmithhunna), meaning: no one had had intercourse with them before their husbands. Al-Farra' said: "al-ṭamth" is deflowering, which is intercourse accompanied by the bleeding of the hymen; one says ṭamathahā, yaṭmithuhā and yaṭmuthuhā, ṭamthan, when he deflowered her. From this comes the saying "a ṭāmith woman," meaning a menstruating woman. Others than al-Farra' disagree with him on this and say: ṭamathahā means waṭiʾahā (had intercourse with her) in whatever manner it occurred. However, al-Farra's statement is more well-known and more common. Al-Kisa'i recited (lam yaṭmuthhunna) with a ḍamma on the mim; it is said: "the woman ṭamuthat (menstruated) with a ḍamma, ḥāḍat." "Ṭamithat" with a kasra is also a dialect form, so she is ṭāmith. Al-Farazdaq said:

"They came to me, not having been deflowered before me, and they are purer than ostrich eggs."

It was also said: "lam yaṭmithhunna" means "had not touched them." Abu ʿAmr said: "al-ṭamth" is touching, and this applies to anything that is touched. One says of a pasture: "No one has ṭamatha (grazed/touched) that pasture before us," and of a she-camel: "No hobbled (ḥabl) animal has ṭamatha her," meaning no tether (ʿiqāl) has touched her. Al-Mubarrad said: meaning no human before them, nor any jinn, has tamed them; and "al-ṭamth" means taming (al-tadhlīl). Al-Hasan recited (jaʾnun) with a hamza.

**Third issue:** In this verse there is evidence that jinn mingle with humans and enter Paradise, and that they will have jinn women there. Ḍamra said: "For the believers among them are wives of the wide-eyed houris: the human women belong to humans, and the jinn women belong to jinn." It was also said: meaning, what God granted to the believing jinn in Paradise of the wide-eyed houris from among the jinn women, no jinn has touched; and what God granted to the believing humans in Paradise of the wide-eyed houris from among the human women, no human has touched; because jinn do not have intercourse with the daughters of Adam in this world. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri.

I say: This matter was discussed in (al-Naml) [see vol. 13, p. 211] and also in (Subhan) [see vol. 10, p. 289], and that it is permissible for the daughters of Adam to be touched by jinn. Mujahid said: When a man has intercourse without mentioning God's name, the jinn coils around his member and has intercourse with him. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Untouched before them by any human or jinn﴾. This is because God, blessed and exalted, described the wide-eyed houris as not having been touched before them by any human or jinn. This informs you that women of the sons of Adam may be touched by jinn, and that the wide-eyed houris are purified and cleansed of this defect. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned it in full, and al-Mahdawi, al-Tha'labi and others also mentioned it. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 58–61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾. al-Tirmidhi narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, a woman from among the women of the people of Paradise, the whiteness of her shins will be seen from behind seventy garments, until the marrow of her shin is seen." And that is because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾. As for the ruby (yaqut), it is a stone which, if you were to insert a thread into it and then strain it, you would see it from behind it [[The addition is from the authentic Sunan al-Tirmidhi.]]. And it is also narrated as a statement of a companion (mawquf). ʿAmr ibn Maymun said: Indeed, a woman of the wide-eyed houris wears seventy garments, and the marrow of her shin is seen through all of that, just as red drink is seen in a white glass. al-Hasan said: They are in the clarity of the ruby and the whiteness of the coral [[So it stands in the manuscripts, but it is known that coral is red.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾ The word (hal) in speech has four meanings: it may mean (qad), as in His saying, exalted is He: (Has there come upon man a period of time?) [[See vol. 19, p. 306]]; it may mean interrogation, as in His saying, exalted is He: (Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?) [[See vol. 7, p. 209]]; it may mean a command, as in His saying, exalted is He: (So will you not desist?) [[See vol. 6, p. 292]]; and it may mean the same as negation (ma fi al-jahd), as in His saying, exalted is He: (Upon the messengers is only the delivery [of the message]) [[See vol. 10, p. 103]], and (Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?). ʿIkrimah said: That is, is the reward of one who says "there is no god but Allah" anything but Paradise? Ibn ʿAbbas said: What is the reward of one who says "there is no god but Allah" and acts upon what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, other than Paradise? It was said: Is the reward of one who does good in this world anything but that good will be done to him in the Hereafter? This was said by Ibn Zayd. Anas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?), then said: "Do you know what your Lord has said?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "He says: The reward of one upon whom I have bestowed tawhid is nothing but Paradise." Ibn ʿAbbas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "Allah says: Is the reward of one upon whom I have bestowed knowledge of Me and monotheism anything but that I settle him in My Paradise and the sanctuary of My holiness, by My mercy?" al-Sadiq said: Is the reward of one to whom I have shown goodness in eternity anything but the preservation of that goodness for him in perpetuity? Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah and al-Hasan said: It is (musajjalah) for both the righteous and the wicked, meaning it is applied to the wicked in this world and to the righteous in the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 55, verses 62–65:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾, meaning: for him, beneath the first two gardens, there are two other gardens. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And beneath them" refers to rank (al-daraj). Ibn Zayd said: "And beneath them" refers to excellence (al-fadl). Ibn 'Abbas also said: "And the gardens are for those who fear the standing before their Lord," so the first two contain palm trees and fruit trees, and the other two contain crops, plants and what spreads out (on the ground).

Al-Mawardi said: It is possible that ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ is for his followers, because their station falls short of his station. One of them is for the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in), and the other is for the everlasting youths (al-wildan al-mukhallad), so that males and females are distinguished by them.

Ibn Juraij said: There are four. Two of them are for the foremost, those brought near (al-sabiqun al-muqarrabun): ﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾ and ﴿two springs flowing﴾. And two are for the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin): ﴿In both of them are fruits, palms and pomegranates﴾ and ﴿in both of them are two gushing springs﴾.

Ibn Zayd said: The first two are of gold, for those brought near, and the latter two are of silver, for the companions of the right. I say: This is the view of al-Halimi, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn, in his book Minhaj al-Din, and he relied on what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, up to ﴿dark green﴾: he said, "Those two are for those brought near, and these two are for the companions of the right." A similar report is narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

When Allah described the two gardens, He pointed to the difference between them. He said of the first two: ﴿In both of them are two springs flowing﴾, and of the latter two: ﴿in both of them are two gushing springs﴾, meaning spouting (fawwaratan). But they are not like the flowing ones, because spouting is less than flowing. He said of the first two: ﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾, so He used the general term and did not restrict it. It is also related from him that the meaning is "gushing with goodness and blessing," and this was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas also, and Anas said: they spray upon the friends of Allah with musk, ambergris and camphor in the mansions of the people of Paradise, as rain sprinkles. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: with all kinds of fruits and water. Al-Tirmidhi: they said with all kinds of fruits and blessings [[In manuscript B: (al-na'im).]], and beautiful maidens, and saddled mounts, and colored garments. Al-Tirmidhi said: this indicates that spraying is more than flowing. And it was said: they well up and then flow.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them is fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first: some scholars said: palm trees and pomegranates are not part of the fruit, because a thing is not conjoined to itself; it is conjoined only to something other than itself. This is the apparent sense of the speech. It was also said: they were singled out for mention because the fruit of the palm is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is both fruit and medicine, so neither was purely for enjoyment (tafakkuh). From this reasoning Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and this is the second issue:

The second: if one swears that he will not eat fruit, and then eats a pomegranate or fresh dates, he does not break his oath. His two companions and the people disagreed with him.

He said: al-Mas'udi related to us from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu 'Ubayda, who said: the palm trees of Paradise are arranged in tiers from their root to their branch, and their fruit is like waterskins; whenever one fruit is plucked, another returns in its place, and their water flows without a trench, and the cluster is twelve cubits long.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 66–69:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them are two springs, gushing forth﴾. That is, gushing with water, related from Ibn 'Abbas. The word for gushing (al-nadh) with the kha' is more common than al-nadh with the ha'. It is also related from him that the meaning is "gushing with goodness and blessing," and this was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas also, and Anas said: they spray upon the friends of Allah with musk, ambergris and camphor in the mansions of the people of Paradise, as rain sprinkles. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: with all kinds of fruits and water. Al-Tirmidhi: they said with all kinds of fruits and blessings [[In manuscript B: (al-na'im).]], and beautiful maidens, and saddled mounts, and colored garments. Al-Tirmidhi said: this indicates that spraying is more than flowing. And it was said: they well up and then flow.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them is fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first: some scholars said: palm trees and pomegranates are not part of the fruit, because a thing is not conjoined to itself; it is conjoined only to something other than itself. This is the apparent sense of the speech. But the majority said: they are part of the fruit, and the reason for mentioning the palm tree and the pomegranate again is their excellence and the fine place they hold relative to fruit, like His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 208]], and His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [[See vol. 2, p. 36]], which has already been mentioned. It was also said: they were mentioned separately because among them at that time the palm tree and the pomegranate were in the position that wheat holds among us, since the palm was the common staple of their food, and the pomegranate was like the fruits [[In the marginal notes of al-Jamal, quoting al-Qurtubi: "and the pomegranate is like the drink," etc.]]. Thus they planted them abundantly, owing to their need for them, while fruits were among the kinds of produce that they admired. So he mentioned fruit first, then mentioned the palm and the pomegranate for their generality and abundance among them, from Medina to Mecca and to the lands of Yemen adjoining them, and so he singled them out in the mention from among the fruits and mentioned fruits separately on their own. It was also said: they were singled out for mention because the fruit of the palm is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is both fruit and medicine, so neither was purely for enjoyment (tafakkuh). From this reasoning Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and this is the second issue:

The second: if one swears that he will not eat fruit, and then eats a pomegranate or fresh dates, he does not break his oath. His two companions and the people disagreed with him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 70–71:

There are two issues here. The first concerns His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them are good (khayrat) and beautiful (hisan) [women]﴾. It means women; the singular of khayrat is khayra, in the sense of "possessors of goodness." It has also been said that khayrat is the plural of khayrah, but it was lightened (fa-khuffifa), as in hayyin and layyin. Ibn al-Mubarak said: Al-Awza'i narrated to us from Hassan ibn Atiyya, from Sa'id ibn Amir, who said: "If one of the khayrat [of the verse] hisan had looked down from the sky, she would have illuminated it, and the light of her face would have overcome the sun and the moon, and the veil [[It is the khimar, and it has been said it is the mi'jar. (al-Nihayah)]] that covers her head would be better than the world and what is in it."

(Hisan) means beautiful in creation. When Allah, may He be exalted, says (hisan), who is able to describe their beauty? Al-Zuhri and Qatada said: (khayrat) refers to good character, and (hisan) refers to beautiful faces. This was also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) through a hadith of Umm Salama. Abu Salih said: because they are virgins, untouched. Qatada, Ibn al-Sumayt', Abu Raja' al-Utaridi and Bakr ibn Habib al-Sahmi read (khayyirat) with shaddah, in accordance with the original form. It has also been said that khayrat is the plural of khayr, meaning "possessors of goodness." It has also been said: chosen (mukhtarat). Al-Tirmidhi said: the khayrat are those whom Allah chose, and He originated their creation by His choice; Allah's choosing is not like the choosing of the children of Adam. Then He said: (hisan), describing them with beauty; so when the Creator of beauty describes something as beautiful, consider what lies beyond that. In the two preceding verses He mentioned that they are (qasirat al-tarf) and (ka'annahunna al-yaqut wal-marjan). So consider the difference between the khayra, who is the chosen one of Allah, and the qasirat al-tarf.

In a hadith: "The hur al-'in, some of them take the hands of others, and they sing with voices that creation has never heard more beautiful nor its like: 'We are the content ones, so we never become angry; we are the abiding ones, so we never depart; we are the eternal ones, so we never die; we are the blissful ones, so we never suffer; and we are the good, beautiful ones, beloved wives of noble husbands.'" Al-Tirmidhi recorded it in substance from the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: When the hur al-'in say these words, the believing women of the people of the world answer them: "We are those who pray, though you did not pray; we are those who fast, though you did not fast; we are those who perform ablution, though you did not perform ablution; and we are those who give charity, though you did not give charity." A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "By Allah, they overcame them."

The second issue: there is a disagreement as to which is more beautiful and more dazzling in beauty, the hur (al-'in) or the human women (al-adamiyyat)? It has been said: the hur, because of their description in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in his supplication over the deceased at the funeral: "And give him a wife better than his wife." It has also been said: human women are better than the hur al-'in by seventy thousand times, and this was related as a marfu' report. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: and Rushdin related to us from Ibn An'am [[He is Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An'am (with the first letter fatha, the nun sakin and the unmarked letter damma).]], from Hayyan ibn Abi Jabala, who said: "Among the women of the world, whoever enters Paradise of them will be preferred over the hur al-'in because of what they did in the world."

It has also been said that the hur al-'in mentioned in the Qur'an are the believing wives of the prophets and of the believers, who will be created in the Hereafter in the best form; this was said by al-Hasan al-Basri. However, the well-known view is that the hur al-'in are not from among the women of the people of the world, but are created beings in Paradise, because Allah, may He be exalted, said: (Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them). Most women of the people of the world have been touched, and because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the least of the inhabitants of Paradise are the women." So not every one of them would have a woman, and He promised the hur al-'in for their collectivity. Thus it is established that they are other than the women of the world.
