Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verse 72–75:

Allah's statement: ﴿Houris, cloistered in pavilions﴾. (Hur) is the plural of ḥawrā’ (a woman with intensely white eyes and intensely black pupils), and it has already been discussed [see vol. 15, p. (80)].

(Maqṣūrāt) means confined and veiled. (Fī al-khiyām) means in the enclosures; they do not roam about the streets. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The khaymah is a hollow pearl." It was also said by Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "It is a farsakh by a farsakh, and it has four thousand doors of gold." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu ʿAbd Allah said, regarding Allah's statement (Houris, cloistered in pavilions): "It has reached us in a report that a cloud rained from the Throne, and the houris were created from the drops of mercy. Then a pavilion was pitched for each one of them on the bank of the rivers, its extent forty miles, and it has no door, until the friend of Allah enters Paradise, whereupon the pavilion is split open to reveal a door, so that the friend of Allah may know that the sight of created beings, from among the angels and servants, has not reached them. Thus she is cloistered, having been confined away from the sight of created beings." And Allah knows best.

He said of the first two (Therein are those restraining their gaze): they restrict their gaze to their spouses, and He did not mention that they are cloistered; this indicates that the cloistered ones are higher and more excellent. Mujahid said: (Maqṣūrāt) means they have been restricted to their husbands, so they do not desire anyone else among them.

In al-Sihah: "qasartu al-shay’ aqṣuruhu qaṣran" means I confined it; from this comes maqṣūrat al-jami‘ (the enclosure of the mosque). "Qasartu al-shay’ ʿalā kadhā" means I did not allow it to go beyond that. A woman who is qaṣīrah or qaṣūrah means one kept confined in the house, not allowed to go out. Kuthayyir said:

"It is you who made every short woman beloved to me, and the short ones do not know of that.
I meant the short ones of the enclosures, and I did not mean the short-stepped, the worst of women, the bahātir."
[Al-bahātir: plural of baḥtarah, with the b vowelled with a damma, meaning a short woman of compact build.]

Al-Farrā’ recited it as qaṣūrah, and Ibn al-Sikkit mentioned it. Anas narrated, saying: The Prophet ﷺ said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I passed by a river in Paradise whose two banks were domes of coral. I was called from it: 'Peace be upon you, O Messenger of Allah.' I said: 'O Jibril, who are these?' He said: 'These are maidens of the houris, the wide-eyed, who asked their Lord permission to greet you with peace, and He permitted them. They said: "We are the everlasting, so we never die; we are the blessed, so we never suffer misery; we are the content, so we never become angry; we are the wives of noble men."'" Then the Prophet ﷺ recited: ﴿Houris, cloistered in pavilions﴾, meaning confined by a confinement of protection and honour.

It is narrated from Asma' bint Yazid al-Ash'haliyyah [in the copies of the original: bint ʿUbayd; the correction is from Tahdhib] that she came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah! We women are confined and cloistered, the foundations of your houses and the bearers of your children. Shall we share with you in the reward?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes, if you treat well [their companionship in marriage and good company] your husbands' kindness and seek their pleasure."

Allah's statement: ﴿Untouched by them﴾, meaning, they have not been touched, as mentioned before. The common reading is (yaṭmithhunna) with a kasra on the mim. Abu Haywah al-Shami, Talhah ibn Musarrif, al-Aʿraj and al-Shirazi, from al-Kisa'i, read it with a damma on the mim in both places. Al-Kisa'i used to kasra one and damma the other, choosing between them: when he raised the first, he kasrad the second, and when he kasrad the first, he raised the second. This is the reading of Abu Ishaq al-Subayi. Abu Ishaq said: "I used to pray behind the companions of ʿAli, and they raised the mim; and I used to pray behind the companions of ʿAbd Allah, and they kasrad it, so al-Kisa'i combined the two traditions." Both are dialects: ṭamuth and ṭamith, like yaʿrushūn and yaʿkifūn. Whoever uses the damma does so to combine the two dialects, and whoever uses the kasra does so because it is the prevalent dialect. He repeated the statement (untouched by them) to clarify that the description of the houris cloistered in pavilions is like the description of the houris restraining their gaze. He says: when they are confined (quṣirna) [in the original texts: idha ḍajirna, etc., and since ḍajar is not permitted in Paradise, we have put qaṣirna in place of ḍajirna], their pavilions are theirs in that state.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 76–78:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Reclining on green cushions (rafraf) and beautiful Abqari carpets.﴾ Rafraf means the mahabis (singular mihbas, a cloth thrown over the back of a bed for reclining on). In al-Lisan it is said: "al-majalis." Both glosses are correct, as the lexicographers attest.

Ibn Abbas said: "The rafraf is the surplus of the bedding and the spreads." He also said: "The rafraf is the mahabis, and they recline on their surplus parts." Qatadah said the same. Al-Hasan and al-Qurazi said: "It is the busut (spreads)." Ibn Uyaynah said: "It is the zarabi (rugs)." Ibn Kaysan said: "It is the marafiq (cushions)," and al-Hasan also said this. Abu Ubaydah said: "It is the border (hashiyah) of a garment." Al-Layth said: "A kind of green garment that is spread out." It has also been said: "The raised bedding." And it has been said: "Among the Arabs, every wide garment is a rafraf." Ibn Muqbil said:

"Indeed we are those who alight, whose sandals are covered
with scattered pieces of fine cloth and rafraf."

These sayings are closely related. In al-Sihah: "The rafraf is green garments from which mahabis are made; its singular is rafrafah." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas also said: "The rafraf is the gardens of Paradise." The derivation of rafraf is from rafa, yarifu, meaning "to rise up," and from it comes rafrafat al-tair, the bird's fluttering of its wings in the air. They sometimes call the ostrich rafraf for this reason, since it flutters its wings and then runs. Also, rafrafa al-tair means when a bird moves its wings around something it wants to land on. Rafraf also means the edge of a tent, the sides of a coat of mail and what hangs from them, its singular being rafrafah.

In the report about the death of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He lifted the rafraf, and we saw his face as if it were a leaf [rustling]," meaning he lifted the edge of the tent. It has also been said that the origin of rafraf is from rafa al-nabtu yarifu, when a plant becomes fresh and lush. This is related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Qutabi said: "It is said of a thing when its water increases from blessing and freshness, to the point that it nearly quivers: rafa yarifu rafifan." This is related by al-Harawi.

It has also been said that the rafraf is a thing on which its rider, when he sits upon it, is made to sway and move back and forth, up and down, like a swing, enjoying it along with his companion. This is what al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said in Nawadir al-Usul, and we have mentioned it in al-Tadhkirah. Al-Tirmidhi said: "The rafraf is of greater value than the bedding. For this reason He mentioned the bedding in the first two verses: ﴿reclining on bedding whose linings are of brocade (istabraq)﴾, and here He said: ﴿reclining on green rafraf﴾." So the rafraf is a thing on which the friend (al-wali) sits and is made to sway, i.e., is carried about this way and that wherever he wishes, like a swing. Its origin is from a rafraf before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It has been transmitted to us in the hadith of the Mi'raj that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached Sidrat al-Muntaha, the rafraf came to him, and he took it from Jibril and it flew with him to the support of the Throne. He said: "It flew with me, lowering me and raising me, until it stopped me before my Lord." Then, when the time came to depart, he took it and it flew with him, lowering and raising, swooping with him until it delivered him to Jibril, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, while Jibril was weeping and raising his voice in praise. So the rafraf is one of the servants before Allah the Exalted, possessing special qualities in the place of nearness and closeness, just as al-Buraq is a beast that the prophets ride, specially designated for that in His earth.

So this rafraf which Allah has subjected to the people of the two gardens nearby is their reclining place and their bedding. It carries the friend over the banks and shores of those rivers wherever he wishes, to the tents of his virtuous, beautiful wives.

Then He said: ﴿and Abqari beautiful [carpets]﴾. The Abqari is patterned cloth that is spread out. So when the Creator of the patterns says they are beautiful, what do you think of those Abaqir!

Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Jahdari, al-Hasan and others recited ﴿reclining on rafarif﴾ in the plural, not diptotic, and likewise ﴿and Abaqiri beautiful [carpets]﴾, the plural of rafraf and Abqari. Rafraf is a collective noun, and Abqari is a singular that indicates the plural, relative to Abqar. It has been said that the singular of rafarif and abaqir is rafrafah and abqariyyah, and that rafarif and abaqir are plurals of plurals.

Al-Abqari means thick rugs, as al-Farra' said. It has been said: they are zarabi, from Ibn Abbas and others. Al-Hasan said: they are busut. Mujahid said: they are brocade (dibaj). Al-Qutabi said: "Every garment and every thing that is fine is called abqari among the Arabs." Abu Ubayd said: "It is attributed to a land where embroidery (al-washy) is made, so every finely woven embroidery is attributed to it." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Until it was as if the gardens of the sandy hill had clothed them
in embroidery of Abqar, arranged and woven."

It is said: Abqar is a village in the direction of Yemen where patterned mats are woven. Ibn al-Anbari said: the original meaning is that Abqar is a village inhabited by the jinn, and every excellent, grand thing is attributed to it. Al-Khalil said: "Every noble, superior, distinguished thing among men, women, and others is called abqari among the Arabs." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "I have not seen an abqari among men who forges his forging," meaning a leader who does great things. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala', when asked about the Prophet's (ﷺ) words "I have not seen an abqari who forges his forging," said: "A chief of a people and their greatest one." Zuhayr said:

"Miserly over them is a gardened abqariyyah,
deserving on a day to attain and to be exalted."

Al-Jawhari said: "Abqar is a place that the Arabs claim is from the land of the jinn." Labid said:

"Elders and youths like the jinn of Abqar,"
(the first half of the line is: "and whoever among their brothers and sons has grown up")

Then they attributed to it everything they marvel at for its skill, excellent craftsmanship and strength, and they said: "abqari," which is both singular and plural. In a hadith: "He used to prostrate on an abqari," meaning these spreads that have colours and patterns. So they said: "Dark oppression is abqari," and "this is the abqari of a people," meaning a strong man. In a hadith: "I have not seen an abqari who forges his forging." Then Allah addressed them with what they were familiar with, saying: ﴿and Abqari beautiful [carpets]﴾. Some recited it as ﴿Abaqiri﴾, which is an error, because the attributed form is not pluralized on its own attribution. Qutrub said: it is not an attributive noun, but like kursiyy and karasiyy, and bakhtiyy and bakhati. Abu Bakr related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿reclining on rafarif green and abaqir beautiful﴾, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Pronouncing the dad in ﴿khudr﴾ with a damma is rare.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾ Tabaraka is from the root of blessing (barakah), a form of tafa'ala, and it has been discussed before [see vol. 13, p. 2].

(Dhi al-Jalal) means the greatness. It has been discussed before, and (wal-ikram) [see p. 165 of this volume]. Amir recited (Dhu al-Jalal) with a waw, making it a description of the name, which strengthens the view that the name is the one named. The rest recited (Dhi al-Jalal), making (dhi) a description of (Rabbika).

It seems he intends the name with which the surah opened, when He said: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾. So He opened with this name, then described the creation of man and jinn, the creation of the heavens and earth and their making, and that ﴿every day He is in a matter﴾. He described His management of them, then described the Day of Resurrection and its terrors, the description of the Fire, then concluded with the description of the Gardens. Then He said at the end of the surah: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, meaning this name with which He opened this surah. It is as if He informs them that all of this came to you from My mercy: from My mercy I created you, I created for you the heaven and earth, the creation and the creature, the Garden and the Fire. All of this is yours from the name al-Rahman. So He praised His name, then said: ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, Majestic in His essence, Generous in His actions.

The reciters did not differ on the description following the name in the raised case (marfu') at the beginning of the surah, and this indicates that what is meant by it is the Face of Allah, which the believers will see when they look upon Him, and so they will rejoice in the good reward, the beautiful meeting, and the excellent gift. And Allah knows best.

All of this is yours from the name al-Rahman. So He praised His name, then said: ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, Majestic in His essence, Generous in His actions.

The reciters did not differ on the description following the name in the raised case (marfu') at the beginning of the surah, and this indicates that what is meant by it is the Face of Allah, which the believers will see when they look upon Him, and so they will rejoice in the good reward, the beautiful meeting, and the excellent gift. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 55, verses 76–78:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Reclining on green cushions (rafraf) and beautiful Abqari carpets.﴾ Rafraf means the mahabis (singular mihbas, a cloth thrown over the back of a bed for reclining on). In al-Lisan it is said: "al-majalis." Both glosses are correct, as the lexicographers attest.

Ibn Abbas said: "The rafraf is the surplus of the bedding and the spreads." He also said: "The rafraf is the mahabis, and they recline on their surplus parts." Qatadah said the same. Al-Hasan and al-Qurazi said: "It is the busut (spreads)." Ibn Uyaynah said: "It is the zarabi (rugs)." Ibn Kaysan said: "It is the marafiq (cushions)," and al-Hasan also said this. Abu Ubaydah said: "It is the border (hashiyah) of a garment." Al-Layth said: "A kind of green garment that is spread out." It has also been said: "The raised bedding." And it has been said: "Among the Arabs, every wide garment is a rafraf." Ibn Muqbil said:

"Indeed we are those who alight, whose sandals are covered
with scattered pieces of fine cloth and rafraf."

These sayings are closely related. In al-Sihah: "The rafraf is green garments from which mahabis are made; its singular is rafrafah." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas also said: "The rafraf is the gardens of Paradise." The derivation of rafraf is from rafa, yarifu, meaning "to rise up," and from it comes rafrafat al-tair, the bird's fluttering of its wings in the air. They sometimes call the ostrich rafraf for this reason, since it flutters its wings and then runs. Also, rafrafa al-tair means when a bird moves its wings around something it wants to land on. Rafraf also means the edge of a tent, the sides of a coat of mail and what hangs from them, its singular being rafrafah.

In the report about the death of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He lifted the rafraf, and we saw his face as if it were a leaf [rustling]," meaning he lifted the edge of the tent. It has also been said that the origin of rafraf is from rafa al-nabtu yarifu, when a plant becomes fresh and lush. This is related by al-Tha'labi. Al-Qutabi said: "It is said of a thing when its water increases from blessing and freshness, to the point that it nearly quivers: rafa yarifu rafifan." This is related by al-Harawi.

It has also been said that the rafraf is a thing on which its rider, when he sits upon it, is made to sway and move back and forth, up and down, like a swing, enjoying it along with his companion. This is what al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said in Nawadir al-Usul, and we have mentioned it in al-Tadhkirah. Al-Tirmidhi said: "The rafraf is of greater value than the bedding. For this reason He mentioned the bedding in the first two verses: ﴿reclining on bedding whose linings are of brocade (istabraq)﴾, and here He said: ﴿reclining on green rafraf﴾." So the rafraf is a thing on which the friend (al-wali) sits and is made to sway, i.e., is carried about this way and that wherever he wishes, like a swing. Its origin is from a rafraf before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It has been transmitted to us in the hadith of the Mi'raj that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached Sidrat al-Muntaha, the rafraf came to him, and he took it from Jibril and it flew with him to the support of the Throne. He said: "It flew with me, lowering me and raising me, until it stopped me before my Lord." Then, when the time came to depart, he took it and it flew with him, lowering and raising, swooping with him until it delivered him to Jibril, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, while Jibril was weeping and raising his voice in praise. So the rafraf is one of the servants before Allah the Exalted, possessing special qualities in the place of nearness and closeness, just as al-Buraq is a beast that the prophets ride, specially designated for that in His earth.

So this rafraf which Allah has subjected to the people of the two gardens nearby is their reclining place and their bedding. It carries the friend over the banks and shores of those rivers wherever he wishes, to the tents of his virtuous, beautiful wives.

Then He said: ﴿and Abqari beautiful [carpets]﴾. The Abqari is patterned cloth that is spread out. So when the Creator of the patterns says they are beautiful, what do you think of those Abaqir!

Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Jahdari, al-Hasan and others recited ﴿reclining on rafarif﴾ in the plural, not diptotic, and likewise ﴿and Abaqiri beautiful [carpets]﴾, the plural of rafraf and Abqari. Rafraf is a collective noun, and Abqari is a singular that indicates the plural, relative to Abqar. It has been said that the singular of rafarif and abaqir is rafrafah and abqariyyah, and that rafarif and abaqir are plurals of plurals.

Al-Abqari means thick rugs, as al-Farra' said. It has been said: they are zarabi, from Ibn Abbas and others. Al-Hasan said: they are busut. Mujahid said: they are brocade (dibaj). Al-Qutabi said: "Every garment and every thing that is fine is called abqari among the Arabs." Abu Ubayd said: "It is attributed to a land where embroidery (al-washy) is made, so every finely woven embroidery is attributed to it." Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Until it was as if the gardens of the sandy hill had clothed them
in embroidery of Abqar, arranged and woven."

It is said: Abqar is a village in the direction of Yemen where patterned mats are woven. Ibn al-Anbari said: the original meaning is that Abqar is a village inhabited by the jinn, and every excellent, grand thing is attributed to it. Al-Khalil said: "Every noble, superior, distinguished thing among men, women, and others is called abqari among the Arabs." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "I have not seen an abqari among men who forges his forging," meaning a leader who does great things. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala', when asked about the Prophet's (ﷺ) words "I have not seen an abqari who forges his forging," said: "A chief of a people and their greatest one." Zuhayr said:

"Miserly over them is a gardened abqariyyah,
deserving on a day to attain and to be exalted."

Al-Jawhari said: "Abqar is a place that the Arabs claim is from the land of the jinn." Labid said:

"Elders and youths like the jinn of Abqar,"
(the first half of the line is: "and whoever among their brothers and sons has grown up")

Then they attributed to it everything they marvel at for its skill, excellent craftsmanship and strength, and they said: "abqari," which is both singular and plural. In a hadith: "He used to prostrate on an abqari," meaning these spreads that have colours and patterns. So they said: "Dark oppression is abqari," and "this is the abqari of a people," meaning a strong man. In a hadith: "I have not seen an abqari who forges his forging." Then Allah addressed them with what they were familiar with, saying: ﴿and Abqari beautiful [carpets]﴾. Some recited it as ﴿Abaqiri﴾, which is an error, because the attributed form is not pluralized on its own attribution. Qutrub said: it is not an attributive noun, but like kursiyy and karasiyy, and bakhtiyy and bakhati. Abu Bakr related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿reclining on rafarif green and abaqir beautiful﴾, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Pronouncing the dad in ﴿khudr﴾ with a damma is rare.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour.﴾ Tabaraka is from the root of blessing (barakah), a form of tafa'ala, and it has been discussed before [see vol. 13, p. 2].

(Dhi al-Jalal) means the greatness. It has been discussed before, and (wal-ikram) [see p. 165 of this volume]. Amir recited (Dhu al-Jalal) with a waw, making it a description of the name, which strengthens the view that the name is the one named. The rest recited (Dhi al-Jalal), making (dhi) a description of (Rabbika).

It seems he intends the name with which the surah opened, when He said: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾. So He opened with this name, then described the creation of man and jinn, the creation of the heavens and earth and their making, and that ﴿every day He is in a matter﴾. He described His management of them, then described the Day of Resurrection and its terrors, the description of the Fire, then concluded with the description of the Gardens. Then He said at the end of the surah: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, meaning this name with which He opened this surah. It is as if He informs them that all of this came to you from My mercy: from My mercy I created you, I created for you the heaven and earth, the creation and the creature, the Garden and the Fire. All of this is yours from the name al-Rahman. So He praised His name, then said: ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾, Majestic in His essence, Generous in His actions.

The reciters did not differ on the description following the name in the raised case (marfu') at the beginning of the surah, and this indicates that what is meant by it is the Face of Allah, which the believers will see when they look upon Him, and so they will rejoice in the good reward, the beautiful meeting, and the excellent gift. And Allah knows best.
